FELICITAS AND HER SEVEN SONS (The martyrs) 
St. Felicitas (Felicity) has been a Christian widow of a noble origin. After 
the death of her husband, she lived serving God, dedicated her life to prayer 
and works of mercy; so that her life and that of her family came to be a role 
model, which had a significant i mpression on so many pagans, that most of 
them converted to Christianity.  The pagan priests complained about her to 
Emperor Antonius Pius (138 -161 AD), accusing her of turning many people 
away from worshipping their eternal gods, and claimed that those gods would 
undoubtedly get mad and harm the city, if not the whole empire. The mad 
emperor ordered Publius, the governor of Rome, to arrest Felicitas and her 
seven sons and to bring them before him. 
St. Felicitas stood before the emperor, who vigorously attempted to apply 
pressure on her, to make her sacrifice to the gods so that he would not have to 
use violence against her and her sons. But she answered him: “Do not think 
that you could make me fear your threats, or to seduce my heart by your nice 
talk; for the Spirit of God inside me will surely strengthen me and will hold 
me fast to have victory over your threats.” The emperor said to her: “How 
miserable you are! If you wish to die, why would y ou destroy your children 
along with you?” The saint answered him: “My children will live forever if 
they are faithful to the True God, but would perish forever if they sacrifice to 
your idols.” 
On the next day, the governor brought Felicitas and her seven sons before 
him, and said to her , “Have mercy on your children, O Felicitas, for they are 
in the peak of their youth.” The mother answered him: “Your compassion is 
deceitful, and your words are evil.” Then, she addressed her children, saying, 
“My children! Look up at heaven, where Jesus Christ and His saints are waiting 
for you. Be faithful in His love. Fight with courage for the sake of your lives.” 
Governor Publius ordered his men to strike her on her mouth, saying to her: 
“How dare you provoke them to disobey the emperor?” He then broug ht her 
children one after the other, attempting to seduce them by promises and by 
threats, to worship the idols, and as they all refused, he ordered to cast them in 
prison. The governor raised their case to the emperor, who ordered killing them 
in different ways: the eldest son Januarius was scourged to death, Felix and 
Philip were beaten with clubs until they died , Sylvanus was thrown down a 
cliff, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were beheaded. Finally, they cut off 
their mother’s head by the sword.  
St. Augustine’ and Pope of Rome Gregory (590-604 AD) commended that 
martyr mother and her seven sons, in the celebration of their martyrdom during 
the 2nd century AD. In his homily, Pope Gregory described what St. Felicitas

her that her salvation is near. On the next day, the governor ordered to resume 
her torture, and then he ordered to cut her head off . At that moment, a lighted 
dove came down on her head, which made many of those present proclaim 
their faith in the Lord Christ. 
 [Butler: September 7] 
 
REGULUS, THE BISHOP , ST. 
St. Regulus (Rieul) is the intercessor of the city of Senlis . He is said to be 
the first bishop in the city , for he lived in the 3 rd century. After that , the 
Cathedral of Senlis was burnt out with all the records of its former bishops . It 
is said that after he proclaimed his faith in the Lord Christ, he set forth to 
France where he preached Christianity. And, he went to Paris to search for the 
relics of the martyrs: St. Denis, St. Rusticus, and St. Eleutherius. Then, he took 
upon himself to convert the inhabitants of Senlis; to Christianity . He reposed 
around the year 250 AD. 
  [Butler: March 30] 
 
REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine . When she was 12 
years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249 -
251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her 
beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making 
her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of 
fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing 
praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she 
holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her 
head off, she walked wi th them singing praise . Finally, when she was 
beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, 
flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she 
was honored by several dioceses. 
 [Butler: October 8] 
 
RESTITUTA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady St. Restituta was a Roman virgin of noble origin, and was 
martyred in the year 271 AD in the town of Sora in Italy. She became the patron 
saint of that city where she was buried . It was said that the Lord Christ 
appeared to her and instructed her to go to Sora, and an angel led her to that

you manage to come here! Who guided you to this convent and carried you all 
that great distance?” When the blessed Sophia told her about what happened 
to her, Akhrosa started to tell the mother-superior and the virgin sisters all that 
God did with Sophia. 
Archbishop Theodorus visits the Convent: 
After hearing all the details and out of fear of the emperor, the mother -
superior sent a message to the archbishop of Jerusalem Abba Theodorus (760-
782 AD), to tell him all what happened. The archbishop instantly came to the 
convent, to see by his own eyes, the saint and the miracle God had done to her, 
and he glorified God for His amazing works. And to spare the city of any 
trouble that might come from the emperor or the own saint's children, the 
archbishop decided to write to them and inform them about ev erything by 
himself. 
Her Strife: 
Sophia started to practice intense asceticism, by going through strenuous 
worship of hunger and thirst; putting before her own eyes, the commandment 
of the Lord Christ: “ Enter by the narrow gate ” (Matt. 7:13). By which she 
lived like the saints who warned us against being compassionate on our bodies. 
She ate only on Saturdays, never ate bread, but fed upon a few wet grains. 
Because of the harsh ascetic life, perpetually watching the nights and 
unceasing prayers, her body became like a dried stick. 
On the 11th day of Toba, she fell sick. The Virgin St. Mary came to tell her 
that after ten days, she would come back to take her to heaven; and that she 
would have the chance to see her children before she would repose.. From that 
moment on, she did not taste food until she departed from her body. 
 
Her Children Came to See Her: 
On the 20th day of Toba, her children arrived in Jerusalem with a message 
from the emperor to the governor to be at their service. The governor and the 
archbishop went out to receive them, and brought them into the city with great 
glory, to worship at the holy locations. 
Then, they went to the convent; and seeing their mother in such a shape, 
with her body shrunken and much changed, they intensely wept and kissed her, 
seeking her blessings. She raised her eyes to heaven, gave thanks to the 
merciful God, who allowed her to see her children before she reposed. 
Telling them all that happened to her, she advised them to offer the true 
worship to God by the spirit, to give money to the convent, and kept counseling

SOPHIA AND HER VIRGIN DAUGHTERS (The martyrs) 
Receiving the Christian Faith: 
This St. Sophia was from a noble f amily in Antioch. She received the 
Christian faith, got married, and gave birth to three girls she named them: Pistis 
(meaning Faith), Elpis (meaning Hope) and Agape (meaning Love). Then, she 
became a widow at a young age. And, when her daughters grew up a little, she 
took them to Rome to teach them the true worship and the fear of God. 
When the sweet fragrance of Christ spread from the life of the mother and 
her three daughters, women came from everywhere to enjoy the spiritual 
encounter with them. And, their house turned into a preaching center for the 
Christian faith. They used to give special care to those souls who failed because 
of the distress. 
Called by Emperor Hadrian: 
On hearing about them, the pagan Emperor Hadrian (117-138) called them 
in. The mother hastened to counsel her daughters and urge them to hold fast to 
their faith in the Lord Christ. She told them: “Beware not to fall and be seduced 
by the vain pleasures of this world and lose the eternal glory. Persevere until 
you come to be brides of your Groom the Lord Jesus Christ and enter with Him 
into Paradise,” The older girl was 12 years old, the middle one was 11, and the 
youngest was 9 years old. When they stood before the emperor, the following 
interrogation took place: “Are you those who fol lowed the vain One and led 
the women of our city astray?” 
The mother answered: “We led no one astray, but we tried to save some 
souls from the vanity of sin and death.” 
“Who are you, old woman? And who are these girls?” 
+ “I am a Christian woman. I worship  my Lord and God Jesus Christ, and 
these are my girls.” 
“Do you know what crime you are committing, O crazy woman? Do you 
know what would happen to those who proclaim this religion? Don't you have 
a heart, to provoke and seduce these beautiful girls?” 
+ “I would be a criminal if I do not testify to my Lord Jesus Christ. I surely 
know that destroying this body is the punishment of those who confess the 
Lord Christ, but I have a desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better 
(Phil. 1:23). And my girls are not less than me in their love of God.” 
“I promise to give them high positions, to treat them like princesses, and to

passages.text:
164 
 
Earlier on, Genevieve 's poor parents received the Christian faith and 
forsook the idol -worship. Then, her father needed her to shepherd his s mall 
flock of sheep, in which the girl found a great chance to spend the whole day 
on the pasture land, practicing a life of prayer and worship of her beloved 
groom Jesus Christ . On the other hand, Genevieve 's mother tried to let her 
daughter stop spending  long hours worshipping God, with no avail . It 
happened that on a feast day, intending to punish her daughter for disobeying 
her, she ordered her to stay home and not to accompany her to church. Pleading 
with her mother with tears, not to deny her the enjo yment of the feast of her 
heavenly groom, the mother in anger, slapped her daughter on the face . In 
return, she was inflicted by blindness for two years. Then, with a contrite soul, 
she gave her daughter some water, asked her to pray o ver it, and then washed 
her eyes with it and God healed her on the spot. When her parents passed away, 
Genevieve went to live with her God-mother in Paris, where she dedicated all 
her time praying and helping others . Yet, she was subjected to ridicule and 
scoffing, even after St. Germanus visited her once again. 
Her Severe Illness: 
Genevieve was inflicted by a severe illness that left her in a coma that lasted 
for three days, and she was on the brink of death . However, God gave her a 
night vision to comfort her, in which she saw the saints in their glory and the 
wicked in their sufferings. She saw her soul had set forth as though to Mount 
Golgotha, to see the Lord  Jesus Christ crucified . This vision became so 
engraved in her heart and gave her the support she needed in her strife.  
Once more, she was inflicted by leprosy , and she was abandoned by 
everyone, but God healed her to become a guide to the virgins in Paris. 
Knowing the Inner Thoughts of Others: 
For her great love of the salvation of her brethren, God granted her the grace 
of understanding the inner thoughts of others and what was going on in their 
minds, and she used that to exhort them to repentance . A girl who vowed 
virginity fell into the sin of adultery, on meeting with the saint, who exhorted 
her to repent. The girl perceived that the saint had complete knowledge of the 
place, date, and time of her sin, and the girl felt shame and did repent sincerely. 
Building a Church: 
Saint Genevieve once revealed to some priests her longing to build a church 
in the na me of St. Dionysius , the martyr. They explained to her that they 
couldn't do that without having the needed building materials. Yet, the next 
morning they, miraculously found all the building materials required in a forest 
nearby, which they used to build that church.

records.question: Who was St. Bishoy?
records.answer:
St. Bishoy, also known as Abba Bishoy, is a revered figure in the Coptic Orthodox Church, celebrated for his deep spirituality and ascetic life. He was born around 320 AD in Shansa, a village in Egypt, and was one of six brothers. After the death of their father, their mother received a divine message from an angel, indicating that one of her children should serve the Lord. She willingly offered all her sons, and the angel chose Bishoy, despite his frail physical condition, affirming that "My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12:9) [3].

At the age of twenty, Bishoy moved to the wilderness of Scetis, where he became a disciple of Abba Bemwah, a follower of St. Macarius the Great. He dedicated himself to a life of prayer and asceticism, spending three years in seclusion without leaving his cell. His commitment to spiritual growth was profound; he engaged in extreme fasting and prayer, even tying his hair to the wall to prevent himself from falling asleep during prayers [3][6].

St. Bishoy is particularly noted for his close relationship with Jesus Christ, which he described as a personal fellowship. He often experienced divine visions and encounters with the Lord, who promised him that his body would never see decay due to his faithful service [2][6]. His life was marked by humility and compassion, as illustrated by his response to the temptation of a woman who had led others astray. He acknowledged the power of temptation and the need for divine assistance, stating, "Nobody can overcome the tricks of Satan in women, except that one whom God is with" [1].

He lived until the age of 97, passing away in 417 AD. His legacy includes the founding of a monastery in his name, where his incorrupt body is preserved to this day, symbolizing his holiness and the grace of God upon him [2][3]. St. Bishoy's life exemplifies the ideals of monasticism and the pursuit of holiness within the Coptic Orthodox tradition, making him a significant saint in the Church.

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls: 
Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world 
and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted 
to Judaism and lived with her . When he happened to encounter some monks, 
he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and 
seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the 
woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning 
to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by 
the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something? ” They answered in 
the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish 
‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish 
woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward 
and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks 
said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My 
children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ 
and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?!  Nobody 
can overcome the tricks of Satan in wo men, except that one whom God is 
with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God 
saved him, and he came back and repented. 
Forsaking Scetis: 
In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of 
‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John 
the Short ’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “ Do you fear death, O man of God? ” He 
answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell 
because of me!” 
St. ‘John the Short ’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba 
‘Anthony’ where he reposed . Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the 
village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain . 
There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and 
sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose , 
and God granted them their wish. 
St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib 
in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle 
of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. 
‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints'  bodies and buried them 
together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El -
Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of 
‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience. 
As the monks knew that the saint would see the Lord now and then; they 
sought from him to intercede for them to enjoy seeing Him as well, so the Lord 
promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren 
greatly rejoiced , and all of them set forth toward the mountain . The saint, 
because of his old age , was at the rear . There, he encountered an old er man 
overcome with weakness and frailty, not able to walk, and none of the passing-
by monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he 
did carry him and walked without feeling any labor . However, the older man 
started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one 
but the Lord  Jesus Christ Him self. He then looked at Him and said: “The 
heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the 
earth; how can a sinner like me carry You? ” To this, the Lord  Jesus Christ 
smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your 
body will never see decay!” Then, He disappeared. St. ‘Bishoy's’ body is still 
kept in his monastery without de terioration up to this very day . Once the 
brethren knew about what happened, they grieved deeply for passing by that 
Old Man and not gaining the blessing of carrying Him. 
An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian: 
By a Divine arrangement,  Mar ‘Ephraim the Syrian ’ came once to meet 
with Abba ‘Bishoy.’ As St. ‘Ephraim’ talked in the Syrian tongue, while St. 
‘Bishoy’ talked in the Cop tic tongue; the later sought from God to give them 
both the ability to understand each other without the need for an interpreter, 
and God granted them that, and they managed to spend a tremendous spiritual 
time together. St. ‘Ephraim’ learned from St. ‘Bishoy’ about the monast ic 
experiences of the Egyptian fathers, particularly of St. ‘Macarius the Great.’  
After a week, St. ‘Ephraim’ left. Then, a brother came to seek St. 
‘Ephraim's’ blessing, but when St ‘Bishoy’ told him that he just left, the brother 
started to run to catch him. St. ‘Bishoy’ called him and said he would never be 
able to because St. ‘Ephraim’ was carried away by a cloud. It was also said that 
St. ‘Ephraim’ has left behind his stick, in front of the cave of St. ‘Bishoy.’ 
Emperor Constantine visited Him:

 [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967] 
 
BISHOY, ST. ABBA 
Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, 
that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had 
a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the 
heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it 
and reign with power and dominion! 
St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El-
Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father 
reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them  up. 
One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: 
‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life. ’” She 
answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” 
The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the 
Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to 
choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made 
perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9). 
In Scetis (Shiheet): 
Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ 
set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disci ple of Abba 
‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he 
worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew 
in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God. 
Life in Seclusion: 
When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ 
and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the 
guidance of God . An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the 
Short’ should remain alone in that location . In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left 
the place forsaking his friend, and d ug for h imself a cave near the southern 
rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’ 
His Strife: 
As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he 
fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it . Then, he used to tie 
the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his 
head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it

BISHAI OF ANTIOCH, ST. 
(The martyr) 
‘Bishai’ (Abshai) was the brother of St. ‘Hur’ (Abahur) of Antioch. He was 
ordained as a priest because of his piety . His brother and his mother went to 
Alexandria, where they were martyred. Their brother, the priest, went there to 
take care of their bodies . Then, he felt the longing to partake in  their crowns. 
So, he set forth to the governor to proclaim his faith, endured sufferings until 
he died. In vain, the governor attempted to burn their bodies. 
The Church celebrates his feast on the 1st day of the short Coptic month: 
‘Nasie’ (the forgotten days). 
 
BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA 
The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit ,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the 
dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile 
river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ 
The three of them were considered among the first monks who became 
disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite). 
He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his 
prayers day and night . He was also known for his love of the book of the 
prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find 
the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him 
ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books 
of the prophets). 
Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the 
nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. 
His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders 
appeared. 
 
BISHAI, ST. ABBA 
The story of this saint reveals the fantastic plan of God for the salvation of 
every soul; how He uses every tool to draw them to Him, and how He sets 
them on the highest level if they receive His call and respond to it. 
This saint, also (called ‘Peter’), was born in the village of ‘Epsona,’ a suburb 
of ‘Akhmim.’ In his youth, he walked in an evil path; but God did not leave 
him there but allowed for him to fall ill, and in a night vision , He revealed to 
him the place of the eternal sufferings  which he was heading to . He bitterly

357 
 
wept, and raised his eyes to heaven and cried out: “My Lord and my God! If 
you heal me of this illness; I shall repent, return to You and worship You 
with all my heart .” ‘Bishai’ (Peter) was healed,  and he  did not forget his 
promise to the Lord, but he was inflamed in his heart with an intense longing 
to experience the monastic life. He forsook the sheep he was shepherding, and 
set forth to the monastery where he met with St. ‘Bigol,’ the uncle of St. 
‘Shenouda’ (who was to become the Archimandrite in Mount Adriba). 
His Monastic Life: 
God used the illness to bring that young man out of the covetousness of the 
body, which would destroy the soul . Once he tasted the real spiritual life, his 
heart got filled with so much joy to set forth firmly and be willing to do so 
many labors enduring daily so many harsh sufferings with a joyful heart.  
He lived with St. ‘Bigol’ in a  fantastic friendship, partaking together in 
monasticism and worship without ever getting bored, watching the nights, and 
opposing the temptations of the devil. 
God granted him an exalt ed capability beyond the limits of human 
endurance; he used to fast, in a way that defied imagination, for a whole month 
not tasting anything, and by a fantastic Divine allowance, he would stand the 
entire night praying. God, in His love, granted him to ha ve the deeds of other 
people revealed before his eyes, which he used to support them on the life of 
true repentance. Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to 
him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings . They benefited greatly by his 
spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the 
world. 
Through the friendship of th is saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when 
the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came 
out in the wilderness in  his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the 
holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the 
presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, 
worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise 
‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12). 
Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near 
the church . I t so happened that while th ey were setting forth to visit A bba 
‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I 
have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.” 
St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by 
St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were 
all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described 
his ascetic life.

up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself 
to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got 
to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most 
of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his 
heart; that it was said that he used to se e the prophet Jeremiah during his 
reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’ 
He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. 
He believed in the saying : “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat. ” (2 
Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich 
man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers 
of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead 
to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the 
man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: 
“You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy .” And, the saint answered him: “Since 
your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.” 
His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus; 
Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on 
a friendship level . He used to see Him, to talk with Him , and to enjoy His 
Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persiste nt in his great 
ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My 
chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and 
behold, I shall always be with you!”  
Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared 
to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint 
answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored 
at all!” 
A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel 
Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain 
to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a 
barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep 
My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: 
“Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the 
Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My 
commandments; I shall save him from all temptations! ” He then blessed him 
and ascended. 
Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted 
him and blessed him . The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with 
water in a basin, then the Lord ascended . St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water 
and left a portion for his disciple . The saint sought from him more than once 
to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check

around, he decided to leave and returned home. He visited on the way some 
Asian cities, in Syria, Mesopotamia, and Nissibin; and God worked through 
him, wherever he w ent. The saint prepared a tomb for himself, on which he 
engraved the sign of the fish, a symbol of the Christian faith, and wrote a 
concise account of God’s work through him in the imperial palace. He reposed 
in the Lord around the year 167 AD. 
[Butler’s Lives of the Saints; Oct. 22] 
 
 
ABSADI, BISHOP OF EBSAY 
(The martyr) 
The word ‘Absadi’ (Bisada) means “the Humiliated." St. ‘Bisada’ was a 
bishop on ‘Ebsay’ (Monshaa), east of ‘Akhmim.’ 
In the days of emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD), ‘Arianius,’ governor of 
‘Ansena’ called him for hearing how he was very vigilant in shepherding his 
people and holding them fast on the Christian faith. 
The bishop called his congregation and advised them to strive. He held a 
Divine Liturgy for them, in which all had the commu nion of the Holy 
Sacraments; then, he bid them farewell and delivered himself to the 
messengers of ‘Arianius.’ At first, ‘Arianius’ treated him decently on account 
of what he saw how awesome the bishop looked. He tenderly asked him to 
obey the orders of the emperor, to spare himself of the ’troubles, but the bishop 
bravely refused to burn incense before the idols. 
Therefore, the saint suffered long by the hinbazeen and by being cast in a 
furnace of fire, where the Lord kept him safe; and he ultimately recei ved the 
crown of martyrdom on the 27th of Kiahk. 
A monastery by the name of St. ‘Bisada’ is still there east of ‘Monshaa.'  
 
ABU AL-HASSAN AL-AMAH 
He was among the 11 th century Copts. He was a secretary of Calipha ‘Al-
Hafez.' He was known for his piety and  his care for reconstructing the 
churches. 
[Iris Habib Al-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church; V. 3; 1981, p. 144]

the Consuls down. The case ended up by punishing and firing the judge and 
the governor, in addition to all those who took part in torturing the saint. 
And to calm the Christians down, the khedive gave the order to hold an 
official funeral for Sidhom Bishai. He also allowed the Cross to be raised in 
public at the front of the saint's funeral procession 1. That display was 
prohibited by the Egyptian rulers for so many centuries. They put the pure 
saint's body in a gasket covered with tin at the expense of the State. His burial 
was celebrated by all sects and was preceded by priests in their priestly attire 
and by deacons carrying banners and crosses. They brought him to the Church, 
where they prayed on him, then buried  his body in a unique tomb on the land 
of the Church, which was originally a cemetery for the Copts. On the night of 
his burial, a shining pillar of light was seen over his tomb and so many people 
took ashes from his tomb for the blessing. 
Finally, the relics of St. Sidhom Bishai were moved to St. George Cathedral 
in Damietta. And, it happened that in the year 1848, they intended to widen the 
church, so they had to move the body of the martyr to a special place on the 
south-west side of the Church, next to that of muåallem Banoub Farag and all 
the rest of his family. There, it remained until the year 1986. The feast of his 
martyrdom was continuously celebrated; until the day the Lord, intending to 
honor His Saint; the committee of the Church decided to move his blessed 
body with a grand celebration into a particular tomb in the court of the Church, 
in the days of the 116th pope Abba Kyrillos VI (1959-1971). One of the toes of 
the right foot of the Saint was placed in a tube in St. Mary Church in Dayrut. 
The Wonders of God through the Saint: 
Many signs appeared from the body of this saint, among which was that a 
rosary which was found in the hand of the saint after moving him, was offered 
to the bishop Abba Aghabius, who carried out the consecration of the blessed 
body. To get its blessing, a brother borrowed it from the bishop, but intending 
in secret to cut a portion of it, St. Sidhom Bishai appeared to him, unknown to 
the man and ordered him to bring it b ack; and so he did, confessed and got 
absolution. 
It happened once that a priest, while sick, came to receive the blessing of 
the martyr, and on leaving, before he reached the door of the Church, he was 
completely healed of his illness. Many other miracles were performed with so 
many visitors of the city and the Church.  
 [The Synaxarion: 17 Baramhat] 
 
1 Later on, this was allowed all over the country during the papacy of the 110th pope Kyrillos IV (1853-
1862), as well as on all the churches and in all the funerals of the Christians…

Abu el-Bishr ibn el-Muqaffaå, the Clerk: 
Sawires ibn el-Muqaffaå ascended the ladder of the State jobs in the era of 
the Ikhshidid dynasty (935-969) who ruled Egypt under the Abbasid Caliphate 
(750-1258), until he became a prominent clerk . He occupied a very high  
position that required a good knowledge of the Arabic language, beside the 
Coptic and the Greek languages. At that time, Sawires was known by the title: 
Abu el -Bishr el -Muqaffaå The Clerk . This did not imply that he had a son 
called El-Bishr, but indicated that he was a prominent and respectable man, as 
it was the custom in those days. 
His Monastic Life: 
After reaching the highest of jobs, Sawires forsook the glory of the world 
and his job, to become a monk in one of Egypt’s monasteries. He managed to 
get much benefit during his monastic life, since he perfected his religious 
education which was based mainly on the Holy Bible and the writings of the 
Fathers. Abu el-Bishr became distinguished in both fields. 
His Knowledge of the Holy Bible: 
According to the researchers, Sawires knowledge of the Holy Bible was 
amazing, so has been his knowledge of the writings of the Fathers; he 
surpassed that of all his contemporaries. This was obvious from his book: “The 
Precious Pearl in Explaining the Religious Doctrine”1 (this is different from 
another book almost with the same title 2), which indicated his extensive 
knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. It could be said that no other author in the 
Arabic language had his knowledge of the Holy Bible; and that his theological 
writings indicated his in-depth knowledge of the works of the Fathers of the 
Church, whether in Greek or Arabic. 
 
Ordained as a Bishop: 
He was chosen as a bishop on the city of El -Ashmonein, which was at the 
time a great bishopric rich in churches and monasteries. Nowadays, it is a small 
village affiliated with the province of El-Roda in the Assiut governorate, to the 
north-west of Mallawy. He was probably ordained by the 59 th Pope of 
Alexandria St. Macarius I (932-952 AD). 
His Debates:

SIDHOM BISHAI (The martyr) 
On the 17th of Baramhat in the year 1561 AM (25 March 1844), the Coptic 
Church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Sidhom Bishai. 
Sidhom Bishai was a trader of wood in the city of Alexandria. He used to 
go twice every year to Damietta to purchase lumber, which was imported 
through its harbor. Being an archdeacon who loved the old churches, Sidhom 
Bishai on hearing that the wooden roof of St. George el -Muzaĥem Church in 
the town of Basat in the district of Sherbin had collapsed; he took on himself 
the responsibility of repairing the damage done and provide d a full ship load 
of wood for that purpose. At the same time, during his visits to Damietta, he 
used to attend the Holy Liturgies in St. George Church. One time, it happened 
that a non -Christian stroked shoulder against him on his way to the church 
aiming to block him from going to the Church. But, seeing how muåallem 
Sidhom Bishai paid little attention to that evil man, he was provoked to anger 
and paid some street boys to insult him. Then, it happened that the Mofti 1 of 
the town was passing by; and thes e boys falsely accused Sidhom Bishai of 
insulting Islam, its “Prophet” and the “Quran.” Those false accusations, 
finding the expected fertile soil in the Moftis ears; he chose two of equally evil 
people around as witnesses. Through these people, they rigged the case against 
muåallem Sidhom Bishai. He was then 40 years of age, well known for 
meekness, kind-hearted and loving for all, not at all expected to utter what they 
falsely claimed that he has done. 
Torturing Him: 
Then, Sidhom Bishai was called in for trial. And, on his way to the court of 
Justice, he was beaten and insulted by every passerby; until he came before the 
judge. The judge ordered torturing him in every way. The mob kept beating 
him violently, plucking the hair of his head, spitting on his f ace, until he fell 
unconscious. When it happened that he was seen in that condition by a 
prominent Copt in the city, called muåallem Banub Ibrahim Farag; Banub 
moved by zeal for his brother, and he cried out loudly at them, saying: “Is it

records.question: Who was St. Anthony, the Father of the Monks?
records.answer:
St. Anthony, known as the Father of the Monks, is a pivotal figure in Christian monasticism and is celebrated for founding the monastic movement. He was born around 251 AD in the village of Kom Al-Aros in Egypt to wealthy parents. After the death of his father, he was deeply moved by the Gospel message he heard in church, specifically the call of Jesus to sell his possessions and give to the poor, which he took as a personal directive. This led him to sell his inheritance, place his sister in a convent, and dedicate his life to God in solitude and prayer [1][2].

St. Anthony initially lived as an anchorite, a hermit who seeks solitude for spiritual growth, in a small hut and later in the inner desert. His life was characterized by rigorous asceticism, which includes practices like fasting, prayer, and manual labor. He sought to live a life of seclusion, often retreating to a cave on Mount Al-Kalzam, where he faced numerous spiritual battles against temptations and demonic forces [3][4]. Despite his desire for solitude, his reputation for holiness attracted many disciples, and he eventually became a spiritual leader, guiding others in the monastic life [2][3].

His teachings emphasized the importance of community and the support of fellow believers, as he often broke his seclusion to assist those in need, including martyrs and fellow monks. St. Anthony's influence extended beyond his immediate followers; he was known for his wisdom and ability to engage with the philosophical debates of his time, even drawing some philosophers to the Christian faith [6][7]. He lived to be about 105 years old, passing away in 356 AD, and his legacy continues to inspire monastic communities worldwide [2][4]. 

St. Anthony's feast day is celebrated on the 20th of Bashons in the Coptic calendar, reflecting his enduring significance in the Church [6].

ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr: 
He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great 
zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then 
he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false 
gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was 
expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop 
assigned him to build a Ch urch, the pagans were stirred up against him and 
killed him. 
ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr: 
St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and 
merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to 
‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. 
The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. 
Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his 
Christ, he ordered him chained and se nt him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of 
Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ 
put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but 
God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' 
where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each 
other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with 
sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint 
received the crown of martyrdom. 
 
ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. 
He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family ’ and 
‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement ’ in the whole world, even though 
there have been some monastic movements prior to his. 
The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around 
the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his 
corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled 
toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the 
gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to 
the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me ” (Matt. 
19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched  his 
life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he 
proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its 
proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister 
also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church. 
St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic 
order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying 
in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out 
to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of 
a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his 
head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned 
to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never 
get bored." That  came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand 
happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life. 
One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash 
their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they start ed to 
undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she 
answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, 
for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint 
said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He 
instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was 
around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to 
practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new 
location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of 
women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts. 
His Order of Seclusion: 
In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with  some 
beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He 
helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he 
was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept 
of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 
4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a 
member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he 
did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when 
Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his 
response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he 
said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of 
kings." However, when he was pressu red, he answered the emperor’s 
message, for the sake of the Church peace. 
5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy 
congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the 
Church. That is why he eventually came  down to help Pope Athanasius 
the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his 
entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants 
came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians 
came back to the Church.

YUSTUS ST. ANTHONY, THE MONK 
The monk Yustus (Justus) St. Anthony was born in the village called Zarabi 
near the M uĥarraq monastery in the province of Assiut in the year 1910 . He 
was given the name Naguib. He worked with his father as a tailor , and he 
learned and mastered the Coptic language . He was ordained as a deacon . 
Naguib went to the monastery of St. Paul in the Eastern desert. There, he spent 
two years as a novice. Then, he moved to the monastery of St. Anthony, where 
he was ordained as a monk in November 1941. 
He was always Expecting the Coming of his Master: 
From the very beginning, in his spiritual strife , he rarely closed his eyes . 
Still, he stayed all night wandering around inside the monastery, as though he 
was anticipating the coming of his Lord. And, whenever he needed some rest, 
he would sit underneath a tree for a short nap. In his early stages of strife, he 
used to lie down on the stem of a fallen tree on the ground, to keep himself 
from a comfortable sleeping, and to remain awake for praying all night long. 
Whenever he met with someone, he would ask him: “ What is the time 
now?” as though anticipating the time of his departure. At the beginning of his 
monastic life, he was fighting against evil thoughts. He was able to overcome 
them by staying awake and reciting the Lord’s Prayer in a loud voice, on and 
on, until they would go away. 
Concerning the Holy Bible, he memorized the Psalms and the epistles of 
Paul the Apostle by heart. And, he loved to read the Holy Bible in the Coptic 
language. Concerning his food, he used to eat just a little amount, mainly from 
the bread crumbles, which would fall off the main dinner table, after he would 
soak them in the water while he would give the rest of his food portion to the 
workers and the stray cats . Monk Yustus always lived poor. He never carried

PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.” 
 [The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25] 
 [Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

According to St. Athanasius, while Abba Anthony was sitting one day by 
his monastery, he saw somebody ascending to heaven, and a multitude of saints 
was welcoming him. Inquiring about him, he was told that he was Abba Amon. 
Thirty days later, some hermits came over from Mount Nitria, to inform St 
Anthony that their father has departed to heaven. 
The C optic Church celebrates his feast on the 20 th of Bashons; and the 
Greek Church on the 4th of October. 
 
 
 
 
AMON, THE RYTHIAN, FR. 
He was called that way because he lived in the region of ‘Rythio’ by the city 
of ‘El-Tur’ in Sinai. He was an Egyptian monk who lived as an anchorite in the 
region of ‘Kanub’ (Abu Quir) at the beginning of the fourth century AD. When 
the persecution was stirred up by Emperor ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD), he was 
exiled to Palestine, and from there, he returned to the wilderness of Sinai. He 
witnessed by himself the invasion of the pagan Arabs on the monasteries of 
Sinai when they destroyed the monasteries and dispersed their monks. At that 
time, Amon set forth to ‘Rythio,' which became the center of a gathering of the 
monks of Sinai. He li ved there for a long time until Rythio ’ was invaded as 
well. And, he then left it and set forth to ‘Manf,' then to Scetis to live among 
its hermits as a disciple to Abba Bemen. When he once asked Abba Bemen 
about the evil thoughts; his answer was: “It is within the power of the enemy 
to bring them to our minds, but it is within our power not to accept them!” 
 
AMON, ABBA 
This saint was the disciple of Abba ‘Poemen’ (Bemoa). He came once to 
visit Abba ‘Sisoes’ (Shishoy) in wintertime. And he noticed that Abba  Sisoes 
was very sad and depressed after he left the life of seclusion in the wilderness, 
so he said to him: “Why are you so sad, O father? How could you have 
managed to live alone in the wilderness at your advanced age? ” The old man 
looked at him with admonishment and said: “What are you saying Amon?! Is 
feeling freedom in the desert not better than anything else?!” 
 
AMON, THE BISHOP OF HERMOPOLIS

at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious 
monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone. 
His Personality and the Role of Nitria; 
Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or 
St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was 
characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away 
from the crowd and refrained from performing a ny miracles, claiming that he 
was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value 
of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in 
that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness 
of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused 
so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted 
to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. 
Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter 
migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba 
Amon. 
St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the 
repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, 
among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also 
found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the 
guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.  
His Miracles: 
Some farmers once came to Abba Amon, carrying a little child mauled by a 
dog and suffering severe pain. The saint asked them: “Why should you come 
to me to do something beyond my worthiness, when, in your hands, you have 
the healing medicine f or this child?! Now, give the stolen cow back to its 
widow owner, and the child will be healed." Having perceived that the saint 
revealed their hidden sin, they presented repentance and gave the cow back to 
its owner. The saint then prayed for the child, and the Lord healed him. 
St. Athanasius told that story about St. Amon: He was once with his disciple 
‘Tadros,’ and they needed to cross a river. Known for his great shyness, he 
sought from his disciple to go away from him, for each of them to take his 
clothes off and swim. Despite doing that, Abba Amon was too shy to take his 
clothes off, even in the absence of his disciple. In the middle of his confusion, 
he found himself all of a sudden on the other shore of the river. When his 
disciple saw him there with  his dry clothes, he was persistence to know how 
he crossed over. The saint told him, seeking from him not to tell it to anyone 
before his repose.

two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court . However, on his way 
to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened 
to be passing by . St. Paul asked himself: “Has t hat rich man taken anything 
from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he 
totally despised the temporal life . His heart was so i nflamed with the Eternal 
inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and  
entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking 
the Divine guidance. 
Then, an angel appeared to St . Paul and guided him to the wilderness in 
the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea . There he 
lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself 
in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration 
of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven . The saint lived 
all that time on that bread with s ome dates from the palm trees or herbs from 
the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring. 
An Encounter with Abba Anthony: 
One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to 
dwell in that wilderness . Then, an  angel of the Lor d appeared to Abba  
Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the 
world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers , God has 
lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain. 
On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St . Anthony set forth  with Divine 
guidance, to the cave of St . Paul. When he got there, St . Paul called him by 
his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their 
lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual  but carrying a whole loaf of bread .

records.question: Who was Pope Cyril I of Alexandria?
records.answer:
Pope Cyril I of Alexandria, also known as "Cyril the Great" and "Cyril the Pillar of Faith," was the 24th Pope of Alexandria, serving from 412 to 444 AD. He is a significant figure in the history of the Coptic Orthodox Church and is best known for his role in the Christological debates of the early Church, particularly during the Second Ecumenical Council held in Ephesus in 431 AD. This council condemned Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, for his teachings that denied the title "Theotokos" (meaning "God-bearer") to the Virgin Mary, which Cyril strongly defended, affirming the unity of Christ's divine and human natures.

Cyril was born between 375 and 380 AD in a wealthy family in Alexandria. He received a comprehensive education in classical and theological studies, which was typical for someone of his background in Alexandria, a major center of learning at that time. His uncle, Theophilus, who was also a pope, played a crucial role in his upbringing and education, ensuring that Cyril was well-versed in the Holy Scriptures and the teachings of the Church Fathers [2][6].

Before becoming pope, Cyril served as a deacon and then as a priest, gaining a reputation for his eloquence and deep understanding of Christian doctrine. His papacy was marked by significant theological conflicts, particularly against the Arians and the followers of Nestorius. Cyril's theological contributions, especially regarding the nature of Christ, have had a lasting impact on Christian doctrine, and he is often credited with shaping the Church's understanding of the Incarnation [5][9].

Cyril's leadership was not without controversy. He faced opposition from various groups, including the Jews of Alexandria, and was involved in conflicts that led to significant unrest in the city. His actions during this period, particularly his expulsion of the Jews from Alexandria, have been subjects of historical debate and criticism [2][3].

Cyril I reposed in peace in 444 AD, and his legacy continues to be honored in the Coptic Orthodox Church, where he is remembered as a champion of the faith and a key figure in the development of Christological doctrine [4][10].

CYRIL II, The 67th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
Pope of Alexandria (1078-1092 AD): 
After the bishops, the clergy and the archons discussed the election of the 
pope in the monastery of St. ‘Macarius’ for two months without coming to a 
decision, they moved to a neighboring monastery ‘Yuannis Kama,’ where they 
selected a saintly elder monk by the  name of ‘Bisus.’ However, he protested 
that he was a common man unfit for that dignity and began banging his chest 
with a stone. He told them that the one who was worthy of this honor would 
be the monk ‘George’ (Gawargius) of the monastery of St. ‘Macarius,’ and that 
he was recommended by the reposed 66th Pope abba ‘Christodolus’ (1046-1077 
AD). So the delegation moved back to the monastery of St. ‘Macarius,’ and 
they found ‘George,’ a middle-aged monk of great sanctity, from ‘Qalaqa’ in 
‘Beĥeira.’ They settled on him as their candidate. They took him against his 
will, clothed him with the patriarchal garb, then they took him to Alexandria, 
where he was formally ordained by the name ‘Cyril II’ in the year 1078 AD. 
He was known as ‘The Sengarian,’ about the cell in which he dwelt as a hermit, 
known by the name ‘Sengara.’ 
He was ordained in the days of the Fatimid Caliph ‘Al-Mustansir’ (1029-
1094 AD), by a decree of a Council of the bish ops and Archons held in 
Alexandria; and all the departments of the government well welcomed his 
ordination. 
The new pope visited the Caliph ‘Al-Mustansir’ in his palace in Cairo, 
where he was greatly welcomed, and the caliph asked him to bless his mother, 
his sister, and the whole palace. The pope also visited the house of his vizier 
‘Badr el-Din Al-Gamali,’ who issued a special decree for his administration to 
execute all the patriarchal wishes.  
This pope sat on St. Mark's throne, while Egypt enjoyed comp lete peace, 
thanks to the rule of vizier ‘Badr el-Din Al-Gamali,’ the Armenian minister, 
during whose time Egypt enjoyed progress and prosperity. The position of the 
church thus became secure, after the hardships it had sustained under Fatimid 
caliph ‘Al-Ĥakim bi-Amr Allah’ (996-1021 AD). 
His Knowledge and Piety: 
Pope ‘Cyril II,’ has been of little education when he was chosen, did what 
the 12th pope ‘Demetrius’ the Vinedresser (188-230 AD) do. And he acquired 
so much learning on his own and was able to leave us a great heritage, which 
testifies to the depth of his knowledge. of God’s grace on him was that, when 
he consecrated the Holy Myron, it flo oded over from the vessel during the 
prayers.

pope ‘John VI’ refused, declaring that he was not the right man for the post.

CYRIL I, The 24th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
This pope was given the title “Cyril the Great” and also “Cyril the Pillar of 
Faith.” Pope ‘Cyril I’ (Kyrillos) name is forever linked to the second great 
conflict about the theologies concerning the identity of the Lord Jesus Christ 
(Christology3). St. ‘Cyril’ led the 2nd Ecumenical Council in Ephesus in the 
year 431 AD, which condemned ‘Nestor,’ the patriarch of Constantinople. 
‘Cyril’ is reckoned as one of the outstanding fathers and theologians of the 
Church. The patristic understanding of the Incarnation owes more to St. ‘Cyril 
of Alexandria’ than to any other individual theologian4. 
His Upbringing: 
Not much is known about his early life. His pious and wealthy grandparents 
lived in the town of ‘Memphis’ which was called ‘Arcadia’ (nowadays ‘Mit 
Rahena,’ south of Giza). On the death of his grandparents, an Ethiopian

nursemaid who was heathen but heartily loved Christianity took care of their 
two children ‘Theophilus’ (Cyril's uncle) and his younger sister (Cyril 's 
mother).  
Once, the nanny took the two children along with her to visit the temple of 
‘Artimus and Apollon. ’ On their arrival, many idols crashed down for no 
apparent reason, and the nursemaid became so afraid. She fled to Alexandria 
with the kids, wher e she met with the 20 th Pope St. ‘Athanasius.’ She was 
surprised when the pope told her about what happened to her in the temple, 
and she proclaimed her faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and got baptized, along 
with the two children. 
‘Theophilus’ was eventually ordained as the 23rd Pope of Alexandria (385-
412 AD), and his younger sister was placed in a house of virgins until she got 
married to a pious man from ‘Mahalet el-Burg’ (Didoyscya), north of the city 
‘El-Mahalla el-Kubra.’ 
Born between the years 375 and 380 AD, ‘Cyril’ got a great deal of learning 
in both the classical and theological knowledge, at the time when Alexandria 
was a great educational center. This in addition to what he was taught by his 
own uncle Pope ‘Theophilus.’ He was raised knowledgeab le in the religious 
books, the Holy Bible, the sayings, and biographies of the fathers. He had, as 
well, the talent of memorizing the Church hymns by heart and singing them 
with his steady voice. 
His uncle made him join the Theological School of Alexandria to study the 
philosophical sciences, which would help him in defending Christianity 
against the heretics and the innovators.  
In the Wilderness of Scetis: 
His uncle sent him, as well, to Abu -Maqar Monastery in the wilderness of 
the Nitrian Valley to becom e a disciple to Abba ‘Serapion,’ who was the 
disciple of abba ‘Maqar the Great, ’ to teach him all the ascetic and 
ecclesiastical knowledge. During the five years that he spent with his mentor 
in the Nitrian Valley, he managed to absorb all the books of the  Church, and 
God granted him the amazing grace of understanding, that by reading a book 
only once, he would be able to memorize it by heart. 
Ordained as a Deacon, then as a Priest: 
After all those studies, ‘Cyril’ returned to Alexandria, to his uncle, who 
commended his great early prominence and ordained him as a deacon. It so 
happened that whenever he started to sing the Holy Gospel in the church, with 
his incredible sweet voice, the believers wished that he would never stop.

did show their consent to ‘Dawud’s ordination out of fear of ‘Abu el-Fetouĥ.’ 
So, ‘Dawud’s ordination was halted. During the following 20 years, which 
the papal throne remained vacant, several of the bishops who opposed the 
ordination passed away. During those long years, however, both ‘Abu el -
Fetouĥ’ and ‘Dawud’ were able to manipulate the church congregation and the 
authorities to emerge as winners in the battle of gaining St. Mark’s throne.  
Since the sultan ‘Al-Kamel’ was in urgent  need for funds to meet the 
expenses of war and repair the harm done to the economy of the land, so he 
ordered his statesmen to bring the Copts to support the ordination of ‘Dawud’ 
as a patriarch, in exchange of taking the money he needed from ‘Abu el -
Fetouĥ’ and ‘Dawud.’ In this way, ‘Dawud’ sat on the patriarch throne by force 
as the 75th pope of Alexandria under the name ‘Cyril III,’ and the ordination 
rite was performed in St. ‘Sergius’ Church in the year 1235 AD, in spite of the 
opposition of most of the bishops and the cry-outs of multitudes of the Copts. 
His Simonism: 
‘Cyril III,’ who was known as ‘ibn-Loqloq,’ needed significant funds, partly 
to enable him to pay the sultan ’s court for its support of his ordination. He 
raised the money by applying the ‘Simoniacal’ practice and by the sale of the 
empty episcopal seats to the highest bidders. Many of these seats had fallen 
vacant during the long interregnum. This practice alarmed the community of 
the faithful, who protested against these practices. The rebellious congregation 
found a leader for their opposition movement in the person of a monk named 
'Imad’ (Hamid) of Anba ‘Macarius monastery. ’ The change was further 
strengthened by a Coptic archon named ‘Saniy al -Dawlah ibn al -Thu’ban,’ 
who insisted that  ‘Cyril’ was pope only by bribery and corruption, and he 
raised serious doubts about the legality of ‘Cyril's ordination. In light of these 
circumstances, it was decided to hold a general council of the clergy and the 
archons to look into the situation and  make recommendations. The Islamic 
administration of the country favored the suggestion and sultan ‘Al-Malik al-
Saliĥ Najm al-Din Ayyubi’ (1239-1249 AD) took the initiative and summoned 
that council where, according to the Islamic historian of the Copts ‘Al-Maqrizi’ 
(1364-1442 AD), the patriarch was sharply criticized. Nevertheless, Cyril, who 
prevailed upon the Coptic scribes of the administration while bribing the 
sultan’s court with 12,000 dinars, was able to swing the verdict in his favor. In 
this way, the opposition to the patriarchal party was stifled, and ‘Cyril III ibn-
Loqloq’ was able to hold his own and rule the church in his approach and a 
wave of relative peace until his death.

CYRIL V , The 112th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
This pope of Alexandria lived in an agitated political atmosphere. However, 
he managed to steer the ship by a patriotic spirit without disregarding the 
spiritual and church aspects.  
In the Paramus Monastery: 
‘Yoĥanna’ was born in the village of ‘Tizmant’ in ‘Beni-Sweif’ province in 
the year 1824, and when he grew up, he was known as ‘Ĥanna al-Nasikh’ (the 
Script) because of his beautiful handwriting. He became a monk in the year 
1844 in the ‘Paramus’ monastery in ‘Wadi al -Natrun,’ by the name of: 
‘Yoĥanna of Paramus.’ At that time, the financial situation of the monastery 
was terrib le, and they had only four monks residing there. Due to the 
tremendous spiritual life and asceticism of the monk ‘Yoĥanna’ and his great 
interest in reading and inscribing, the Holy Bible drew so many to the monastic 
life. Two years after he became a monk, his fellow monks sought from the pope 
to have him ordained as a priest. The 111 th pope ‘Demetrius II’ (1862-1870) 
ordained him. When the pope sensed his seriousness and spirituality, he was 
planning to keep him in the patriarchate to help him. However, th e ‘Paramus’ 
monks wrote to the pope asking him to send their priest back to them, and he 
went along with their request. 
Again, the pope called Fr. ‘Yoĥanna’ later on, ordained him as a Hegumen 
(proto-priest), and kept him to serve at the Cathedral of ‘Azbakieh’ in Cairo. 
When again the monks wrote to the pope begging to send him back to them, 
he still responded to their request. 
Ordained as Pope of Alexandria (1874-1927): 
After the repose of pope ‘Demetrius II’ in 1870, the papal throne remained 
vacant for four years and nine months, although everybody was expecting that 
Fr. ‘Yoĥanna of Paramus’ would fill it. 
Finally, the ‘General Congregational Council, ’ which ran the church ’s 
financial affairs, presented a request to the government about his ordination. 
Then, Hegumen ‘Yoĥanna’ was ordained as a patriarch on the 1st of November 
1874, by the name of Pope ‘Cyril V .’ The sons of khedive attended the 
celebration: ‘Ismaåil Pasha, ’ ‘ Tewfik Pasha, ’ ‘ Hussein Pasha Kamel, ’ and 
‘Hassan Pasha;’ along with a number of government ministers. 
The Political Situation: 
Due to huge accumulated debts after the Suez Canal construction, Egypt at 
that time was passing through a horrible political struggle. Khedive ‘Ismaåil 
Pasha’ (1863-1879) was exiled, and his son ‘Tewfik Pasha’ ruled in his place.

499 
 
St. ‘Cyril’ was born in Jerusalem or one of its villages in the year 315 AD. 
He has ordained as a deacon in the year 335 AD, then as a p riest in the year 
345 AD. Despite his young age, he was entrusted by the bishop to teach the 
catechumens to qualify them to get the Sacrament of Baptism; and to give 
sermons on the Sundays and feasts. 
Ordained as a Bishop (350-386 AD): 
In the year 348 AD, because of St. ‘Cyril's’ knowledge and piety, he was 
chosen by ‘Acacius,’ the bishop of Caesarea, to succeed Abba ‘Maximus III’ 
the bishop of Jerusalem ( 334-348 AD). Unfortunately, as ‘Acacius’ was an 
Arian, doubts dwelt upon ‘Cyril.’ However, he soon ente red into severe 
conflict with ‘Acacius’ and the Arians, while defending the Orthodox teachings 
concerning the Divinity of the Lord Jesus Christ. 
His Disagreements with ‘Acacius,’ Bishop of Caesarea: 
A controversy happened between him and ‘Acacius’ bishop of Caesarea, 
concerning their dioceses and “Who has the priority right over the other .” St. 
‘Cyril’ assumed that the priority would be to his diocese ‘Jerusalem,’ being the 
See of St. ‘James,’ one of the twelve apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ.  
Taking the chance of that, St. ‘Cyril’ took the liberty of selling some of the 
Holy Vessels of the church to feed the needy during a severe famine that dwelt 
upon Palestine. Because of that, ‘Acacius’ tried here and there until he got a 
decree to exile St. ‘Cyril’ out of ‘Jerusalem,’ without giving him the chance to 
defend his case. 
In the year 359 AD, St. ‘Cyril’ appealed before the Council of ‘Selucia.’ As 
‘Acacius’ was called to attend, and he declined, the Council deposed him and 
restored ‘Cyril’ back to his throne. 
‘Acacius,’ supported by the Arian bishops, soon seduced Emperor 
‘Constantius II’ (337-361 AD) to hold a Council in Constantinople in the year 
360 AD, which issued a decree to exile ‘Cyril’ again. 
When ‘Constantius II ’ died, and his successor ‘Julian’ ( 360-363 AD) 
ordered the return of the exiled bishops to their thrones, St. ‘Cyril’ returned to 
Jerusalem in the year 362 AD, and resumed shepherding his people faithfully 
and uprightly. 
Resuming his opposition against the Arians, they sought from the Arian  
Emperor ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD) to annul the decree of the return of the exiled 
bishops to their thrones; and ‘Cyril’ was exiled for the third time. When 
Emperor ‘Valens’ died in the year 378 AD, he was followed by Emperor 
‘Theodosius I’ (379-395 AD), who r eleased the saint from exile and held a 
Council of 150 bishops in Constantinople in 381 AD against ‘Macedonius.’ 
That council was attended by St. ‘Cyril,’ who opposed ‘Macedonius,’

governor about the work of God with his son, he ordered to burn them together, 
and they received the crowns of martyrdom. 
Here, 640 pagans shouted aloud, proclaiming their faith in the Lord Christ, 
and they all, as well, received the crowns of martyrdom. 
 
DIOSCORUS I, The 25th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
St. ‘Dioscorus’ was the 25th Pope on the See of St. Mark (444-454 AD). He 
was a revered man, who beside s his spirituality and in-depth theological 
knowledge, enjoyed courage, steadfastness in the truth, and the willingness to 
sacrifice until death for the sake of the Orthodox Faith . Therefore, the 
Orthodox Church gave him the title: “The Hero of Orthodoxy.” 
His papacy started in a relatively peaceful time of the church, although he 
encountered many troubles after the death of emperor ‘Theodosius II’ (402-
450 AD) in the year 450 AD . This emperor, who was called by the church: 
‘The Orthodox Emperor ,’ was replaced by an unfriendly emperor ‘Marcian’ 
(450-457 AD) and his wife ‘Pulcheria.’ At that time, the theological debate 
about the issue of “Christology”1 flared up, after had been somewhat settled 
during the first three Ecumenical Councils. On the arrival of Emperor Marcian, 
plots were woven against the Church of Alexandria and her great bishops; these 
plots were led by ‘Leo I,’ the Pope of Rome (440-461 AD), who was a close 
friend to the emperor ‘Marcian’ and his wife. 
The Greatness of the Alexandrian Church: 
St. ‘Dioscorus’ succeeded the 24th Pope St. ‘Cyril the Great ’ on the 
Alexandrian Throne of the See of St. Mark . He should be regarded as one of 
the chief architects of Coptic Christianity and the Alexandrian Church. Owing 
to his devotion to the faith and his genuine character in defense of his high 
principles, he was chosen by Pope ‘Cyril I ’ (412-444 AD) to be his close 
companion in his religious meetings. ‘Cyril’ made him an archdeacon, and he 
served as the dean of Alexandria ’s Catechetical School. Pope ‘Cyril’ became 
‘Dioscorus’ chief mentor, and together they attended the famous Ecumenical 
Council of Ephesus I in 431 AD, where Cyril’s Christological formulas were 
accepted as the Orthodox definition of the Nature of Jesus Christ . We 
might assume that the archdeacon ‘Dioscorus’ must have contributed in the 
formulation of those decisions of the Council, being a power behind the throne 
of Pope ‘Cyril’ who presided over the Council . It was on such occasions that 
the personality of ‘Dioscorus’ became recognized within his church and

records.question: Who was St. Takla Haymanot?
records.answer:
St. Takla Haymanot is a significant figure in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, revered as one of the pillars of Ethiopian monastic life. He lived from 1215 to 1313 and is celebrated for his deep commitment to a life of purity, chastity, and asceticism. His early life was marked by a desire for celibacy, which he maintained even when pressured by his parents to marry. After marrying, he lived with his wife in a brother-sister relationship until her death, after which he was ordained as a priest by the metropolitan of Ethiopia, Abba Girguis II [1][4].

His transformation into a saintly figure began when the Archangel Michael appeared to him, urging him to abandon hunting and dedicate his life to prayer, studying the Holy Bible, and teaching. He was also blessed with the gift of healing and performing miracles, which he used to preach the Gospel and combat idol worship in Ethiopia. St. Takla Haymanot traveled extensively to spread Christianity, facing significant opposition but supported by divine miracles [1][2].

St. Takla Haymanot founded a monastery in the Amhara region, where he lived a life of asceticism and became a spiritual father to many monks. His monastery became a center for preaching and spiritual growth. He was known for his humility and compassion, even raising the monastery's abbot from the dead through prayer, which further solidified his reputation as a miracle worker [2][3]. 

Throughout his life, he demonstrated a profound commitment to serving others, practicing asceticism, and fostering a community of faith. His legacy continues to inspire many within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, where he is venerated as a saint and a model of Christian virtue [4].
