(311-313 AD).  
A group of ninety-seven confessors: men, women , and children, were 
brought to the governor , and  he ordered  the executioners to burn the  
believers' left feet using red hot heated iron and to pluck out their right eyes 
then sear them with red hot metal. Afterward, he sent those courageous 
confessors to work as slave laborers in the mines of Lebanon. 
Another group from Gaza was arrested while gathering in prayer and 
listening to the Word of God. Among them was a girl named Thea (Tia), who 
rebuked the governor when he threatened to have her raped in public , and he 
ordered that she would be whipped and t ortured. When another girl from 
Caesarea of Palestine, named Valentina saw that, she rushed through the 
crowd to tell the governor: “Until when will you torture my sister?”  She was 
arrested and was taken to the temple of the idols . There, she kicked the al tar, 
and the governor ordered tying the two girls together and burning them alive. 
At the same time, the head of a Christian man name d Paul (Paulus) was 
cut off because he held fast to his f aith. That man showed an amazing love in 
the moments before his ma rtyrdom. After he requested the permission of his 
executioner, he stood up and with contrition prayed with a loud voice to God 
for his companions to support them in the moments of their s uffering; for the 
spreading of f aith; for t he sake of all who were pr esent and for that of the 
emperor, the governor and all the officials.  
His sufferings drew him to think not of himself but of the others, even the 
opponents and the persecutors, to pray to God to grant them Salvation. 
 [Eusebius: Ecclesiastical History, ch. VIII] 
 
PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA 
Through Divine care , St. Abba Anthony the Great the Father of the 
Monastic family and its founder in the whole world, encountered this St. Paul 
who preceded him by long years in monastic life in the wilderness, where no 
one but God knew anything about him . God kept sustaining him by half a 
loaf of bread, carried to him by a raven every day all along many decades; in 
which God smelled the sweet fragrance of his prayers and praise, to call him: 
“My beloved Paul.” 
His Upbringing: 
St. Paul the 1st hermit was born in Alexandria around the year 228 AD. His 
father passed away leaving a great wealth for him and for his older brother 
Peter. However, Peter conspired to acquire the greater portion of the 
inheritance for himself, and  when the disagreement escalated between the

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 381
passages.text:
381 
 
AD; St. Abba Bishoi fled the area and went to mount Anesna in Upper Egypt. 
There, he met with Abba Paul the H ermit and they both had an amazing 
spiritual friendship, that an angel appeared to St . Paul, saying: “ Your body 
will be with that of Abba  Bishoi.” (The two bodies are still together in one 
tube in the Monastery of Abba Bishoi up to this very day) . It was said that 
later on when the bishop of Anesna  decided to move the body of Abba  
Bishoi; his boat did not move until a hermit name d Jeremiah told them about 
the promise of the Lord to Abba Paul, so they brought the body of Abba Paul 
to the boat and they moved them together to the Monastery of Abba  
Shenouda in Akhmim . Later on, the bodies of these two saints were moved 
again together in the days of the 52 nd Pope Yusab I in the 9th century (831-
849 AD) to the Monastery of Abba Bishoi in the Scetis. 
The bodies of the two saints were kept in one tube; and this is a testimony 
of the spiritual friendship full of love that bound the two saints together; that 
even death could not separate them. This is not on the le vel of this mortal 
world but the level of the Eternal glory of both the body and the soul. 
Abba Paul was known for his great love of worship, particularly for the 
perpetual prayers, as well as his serious asceticism, that his disciple Ezekiel 
told about him that he faced death six times because of his harsh asceticism. 
He lived in solitude as a herm it, in perpetual strife, that the Lord  Jesus 
Christ appeared to him saying: “ Enough labor, My beloved Paul”.  St. Abba 
Paul answered Him: “ O my Master, let me exhaus t my body for the sake of 
Your Name; as You have done for the sake of mankind. Even though You are 
God, You delivered Yourself for our sake, we who are unworthy.” 
 [O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt; p. 223-4] 
 
PAUL THE GREAT, ST. 
St. Paul the Great once said: “The monk who cares for the few things he 
has in his cell, will be mocked by the demons . Personally, I suffered from 
such a situation.” This St. Paul (Boulus) was from Galatia, a Roman province 
in Anatolia (modern central Turkey). 
[Boulus the Confessor: cf. the Biography of ‘Ur’ (Hur), Isaiah, Boulus & Nobi] 
 
PAUL (The martyr) 
The historian Eusebius mentioned the details of what  he witnessed of 
violence and brutality in Caesarea of  Palestine against the believers , in the 
year 324 . These tortures were inflicted by the governor of Palestine 
Firmilianus, the successor of Urbanus, in the days of E mperor Maximinus II

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 384
passages.text:
384 
 
of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St . Anthony what to 
do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on 
the ground and they dug the grave with their claws ; according to St. Antony's 
directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body. 
St. Anthony carried the garment of palm t ree fibers and presented it to 
Pope Athanasius who gr eatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every 
year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany , and Resurrection . Many signs 
were shown by that garment. 
In the location where St . Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery 
was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise 
for the Lord. 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.” 
 [The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25] 
 [Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

385 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
One of the desert fathers told this story about a monk by the name of Paul  
(Boulus) from somewhere in Lower Egypt and he lived in Thebes:  
He used to hold a serpent by his bare hands and split it into two . Some of 
the brethren made metanoia before him, and said: “Tell us brother; what did 
you do that made you qualified for such a marvelous grace ?” He answered 
them: “Forgive me, fathers. Once the man acquires purity, everything would 
submit to him and obey him. Like the way , Adam was in Paradise before he 
disobeyed the Divine commandment.” 
 [Light Publications: Sayings of the Elder Fathers, 1983, p. 258 (Arabic)] 
 [Bendicta Ward: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers] 
 
PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST. 
This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of 
God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 
60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer 
who got married to a very beautiful girl . After living together for so many 
years, he started to take notice o f so many rumors about his wife' s evil 
behavior. However, whenever he inquired fr om her about the matter, she 
would pretend to be a pure woman . Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the 
evil act . On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba 
Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples. 
Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony 
advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be 
difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age . Before his 
persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in  the valley to practice 
with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not 
leaving that mountain. 
Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; 
and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance , and obedience . Among 
those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching 
him lest he would collapse. He s ought from him to  remain a whole week 
outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without 
leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, 
to loosen it and weave it anew . In all that he was obedient, worked with joy 
and extreme simplicity. 
On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted 
him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way 
between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church – Volume 1  
666 
In the apostolic age, many practiced a kind o f monasticism, seeking to enjoy the 
perfection of the Gospel. The eschatological direction of the Church made the believers long 
for the coming of their Bridegroom, so some preferred to live a life of virginity, consecrating 
all their time for worship to p repare themselves for the heavenly wedding. In the second 
century, the Christian virgins in Smyrna and Corinth used to walk in liturgical processions 
behind the priests and in front of the widows. Moreover, many groups of virgins were found 
living in Alexandria and in many cities around the world. Articles about virginity represented 
an essential aspect of the writings of the Church Fathers in the first three centuries. 
Virgins used to live together, while men preferred to leave the cities to live in simple huts 
in villages and were often called “consecrated.” Some people felt a thirst for the angelic life 
so they fled to the wilderness. We know of only a few of these, such St. Paul the Hermit who 
lived in the wilderness for almost ninety years (between 250–340 A. D.). 
St. Anthony established the monastic movement and is considered the father of all monks 
in the entire world, even though many preceded him. This is because of his strong relationship 
with St. Athanasius, who wrote about him to the Roman world. It is also because he opened 
his cave after twenty years of solitude to disciple monastic leaders, converse with 
philosophers in the simplicity of his faith, and receive rulers. He had an active role in the 
Church and went to Alexandria to support the martyrs and stand against the Arians. 
St. Pachomius, founder of cenobitic monasticism, felt that the order of solitude may not 
work for all those who want to become monks, so he started a monastic community within 
the walls of monasteries, and the hermits praised him for doing so. 
St. Macarius the Great, St. Ammonas and others started the order of communities (or the 
semi-eremitical order). Many came from around the world to practice the ascetic life in 
Egypt, and to write about it and take these orders back to  their countries. It is important to 
note that the leaders of the three orders were not biased for their monastic styles, but instead 
they used to visit each other and praise each other’s orders. 
The monastic movement of women started side by side with tha t of men, and monks 
helped build convents. Female leaders arose and had great influence, like Amma Sarah, 
Amma Theodora, and Amma Syncletica. Moreover, some Egyptian and foreign women were 
disguised in the apparel of men and led ascetic lives in monasterie s of men, and their 
asceticism, struggles, and spirituality exceeded many. 
875. Who were the most important monastic leaders? 
St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit):  St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 
375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and 
Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his 
parents. During the persecution of  Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness 
after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years

passages.text:
380 
 
West (Gaul, Britannia, and Hispania) was for Constantine II (337 -340 AD). 
Emperor Constantius II  was inclined toward Ariani sm, so he exiled the 
patriarch Paul I to set Eusebius of Nicomedia  in his place on the throne of 
Constantinople. However, Eusebius died in the year 341 AD and the church 
was saved from his evil plots. While the Arians set the deacon Macedonius as 
his successor; the Orthodox congregation brought back their legal patriarch . 
When the two factions fought against one another, with dead and wounded on 
both sides; the emperor sent his high army commander to establish peace, but 
when he was killed, the emperor came by himself and forgave everybody. Yet 
because of his inclination toward the Arians, he exiled the patriarch Paul I for 
the third time. 
The Arians found their chance to spread their heresy; and Macedonius 
spread a new heresy, by which he denied the Divinity of  the Holy Spirit . 
Patriarch Paul I feeling his responsibility toward his people ; he had to return 
to Constantinople to hold th e congregation on the Orthodox F aith and to 
counter the other vanities. When the emperor heard about that, he sent some 
people to get hold of him in secret, and he was taken in chains to be exiled in 
Singara in Mesopotamia. Then, he was taken back to Homs  (Emesa) and was 
left there. During all that, he suffered his fourth exile with thanksgiving. 
When the Pope of Rome Julius I  (337-352 AD) heard about St . Paul's 
latest exile; he sought the help of Constans I the emperor of Italy and Africa. 
That emperor loved the c hurch, and he intervened with his brother 
Constantius II  to bring back the exiled bishops . Then, he held a Church 
Council in Sardica headed by P ope Julius I in the year 343 A D, in which he 
excommunicated Macedonius and the Arians . Constantinople received its 
patriarch with great joy, and St. Paul I did his best to shepherd his flock. 
When emperor Constans I was assassinated, the Arians found their chance 
to slander Pope Paul I and to accuse him of heresy and evil practices . They 
eventually managed to get hi m exiled for the fifth time to Cucusus  in the 
mountains of Cappadocia ( in Armenia Minor), where he reposed in the Lord 
in the year 351 AD, as a result of what he suffered of labors, hunger , and 
thirst; enduring them all with joy. 
The Latin Church celebrates his feast on the 7th of November. 
 
PAUL OF TAMOUH, ST. ABBA 
The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of this saint on the 7th of Baba, and 
seeks his prayers in the commemoration  of the saints in the Liturgy, along 
with St. Ezekiel his disciple. 
After the devastation of the wilderness of the Scetis around the year , 408

337 
 
memorial on the 2nd day of the Coptic month of Mesra.  
 
PAESIUS (The martyr) 
Paesius and Paesi were among the common names of the early monks and 
martyrs. We can mention few of them: 
1- St. Paesius: an Egyptian martyr who offered his life together with others 
as a sacrifice to God in the 2nd year of the persecution stirred up by 
Emperor Diocletian  (284-305 AD).  They were tortured by Urbanus, the 
governor of Caesarea of Palestine [Eusebius: Martyrs of Palestine]. 
2- Martyr Paesi  (Paesius/Isi): brother of martyr Takla; two Egyptians (8 
Kiahk) from Abisir, west of El-Ashmonein (see Isi). 
3- St. Paesius, brother of Abba Isaiah, the Scetic (see Isaiah). 
4- St. Paesius, brother of Abba Bemen, the hermit; also called Paul, one of 
seven brothers. 
5- St. Paesius, brother of Abba  Paul and Abba Bishoi. Sometimes the name  
Paesius is mentioned instead of Bishoi. 
 
PALAMON, THE HERMIT, ST. ABBA 
This saint Palamon was mentioned on the 20 th day of Toba in the 
Synaxarion published by Rene Basset . He is a different saint from  Abba 
Palamon, the mentor of St. Pachomius, the Father of the Koinonia.  
In the Eastern Wilderness: 
We do not know a lot about this saint, except for his story , which showed 
the bitter war that Satan would raise against everyone, particularly those who 
achieve a high spiritual level . This father was earnest in his spiritual strife, 
never known to laugh since his youth . Yet the enemy planned to push him to 
the pit to destroy him completely if it was not for the e levated care of God 
Almighty. 
It was said that he once came out from his cave on the eastern side of the 
mountain, carrying a little of his handwork to sell it i n the countryside . It 
happened that he lost his way in the middle of the wilderness and could not 
find any sign that would lead him in the right direction . He remained that 
way for a whole week without food or drink in the deadly heat of summer . 
When he was on the brink of death, he cried out loud: “My Lord Jesus Christ, 
help me .” He instantly heard a voice telling him: “Have no fear, for the 
enemy will have no power on you because you remember Me . Get up, walk 
toward the south, until you meet a true elder monk named Thallason, as solid 
as a stronghold . Tell him about how Satan seduced you and about the great

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 379
passages.text:
379 
 
Berba (pagan temple) and a fire was ignited underneath them . However, they 
were not harmed and the fire almost consumed  the temple. Here, the priests 
of the idols intervened and begged the governor to get rid of them by having 
their heads cut off, which he did . Afterward, God performed so many signs 
and healings from the bodies of these two saints. 
 
PAUL I, THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE 
With jealousy on the Orthodox Faith, St. Paul I, the patriarch of 
Constantinople (337-351 AD) stood against the Arian heresy that denied the 
Divinity of the Lord  Jesus Christ. He had a close relationship with  the 20th 
Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD) and the Pope 
of Rome, St. Julius I (337-352 AD). St. Paul I  was exiled five times during 
his patriarchate, these were plotted by Eusebius of Nicomedia and 
Macedonius, the denier of the Holy Spirit. 
This saint was bo rn in Thessalonica at the end of the 3rd century. He was 
raised on lovi ng God and holding fast to the f aith. When he moved to 
Constantinople, its p atriarch Alexander (314 -337 AD) ordained him as a 
priest, after observing how he led a tru ly pious life, along with great 
knowledge and strong faith . As a priest, he was loved by the congregation , 
and when the patriarch felt that his departure was close, he gave his counsel 
to choose the priest Paul (Boulus) as his successor. 
His Patriarchate:  
St. Paul was chosen as an archbishop of Constantinople in the year 337 
AD. This was the start of his struggle in bearing his Cross . His troubles were 
mainly caused by the heretics who focused on opposing him until the 
moment of his departure from this world . Eusebius of Nicomedia, w ho was 
cherished by the emperor's sister, was able to convince E mperor Constantine 
the Great (306 -338 AD) to exile th is saint after he and his collaborators 
presented so many false claims and reports that stirred up the emperor against 
him. However, after his exile, they tried to convince the emperor to get 
another patriarch to replace him; but Constantine refused to do so . The saint 
remained in exile until  Emperor Constantine passed away in the year 338 
AD, then he returned to his  throne; as did St . Athanasius the Apostolic, St. 
Eustathius of Antioch, St. Marcellus bishop of Ancyra and others. 
His Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Exiles: 
Before he died, E mperor Constantine the Great divided his empire on his 
three sons: The East an d Constantinople  was the portion of Constantius II 
(337-361 AD); Italy and Africa that of Constans I (337 -350 AD); and the

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 383
passages.text:
383 
 
two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court . However, on his way 
to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened 
to be passing by . St. Paul asked himself: “Has t hat rich man taken anything 
from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he 
totally despised the temporal life . His heart was so i nflamed with the Eternal 
inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and  
entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking 
the Divine guidance. 
Then, an angel appeared to St . Paul and guided him to the wilderness in 
the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea . There he 
lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself 
in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration 
of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven . The saint lived 
all that time on that bread with s ome dates from the palm trees or herbs from 
the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring. 
An Encounter with Abba Anthony: 
One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to 
dwell in that wilderness . Then, an  angel of the Lor d appeared to Abba  
Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the 
world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers , God has 
lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain. 
On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St . Anthony set forth  with Divine 
guidance, to the cave of St . Paul. When he got there, St . Paul called him by 
his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their 
lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual  but carrying a whole loaf of bread . 
St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all 
along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, 
but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.” 
At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to 
bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius 
the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching . Abba 
Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment , and headed back to 
St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his s oul to 
Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God. 
On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling . 
For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to 
finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely 
mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.  
When St. Antony wanted to bury St . Paul, he wondered how he could dig 
the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body

records.question: Who was St. Abanoub, and how old was he when his parents died?
records.answer:
St. Abanoub was a young Christian martyr who lived in the 4th century. He was born in Nehissah, in the city of Talkha, to pious parents who instilled in him strong Christian values and a love for God and the Holy Bible. Tragically, he lost both of his parents when he was only 12 years old, which left him deeply sorrowful and earned him the title "the lamented boy" due to his prolonged grief over their loss [1].

Despite this early tragedy, St. Abanoub's faith remained strong. His parents' piety and prayers likely continued to support him spiritually even after their passing. After their death, he was inspired by a priest's sermon encouraging the congregation to endure suffering for their faith. This motivated him to seek God's guidance and ultimately led him to openly declare his Christian faith, despite the dangers it posed during a time of persecution against Christians [1][4]. 

St. Abanoub's life is marked by his steadfastness in faith, as he faced severe tortures for refusing to renounce Christianity, ultimately leading to his martyrdom. His story reflects the profound impact of early loss and the strength derived from faith and community support.

passages.text:
33 
 
 
ABANOUB EL-NEHISSY 
(The martyr) 
St. Abanoub was born in Nehissah, in the city of Talkha in the 4th Century. 
His parents were pious loving parents who raised him with Christian values 
and planted in him the love for God and the Holy Bible. He was only 12 years 
of age when both his parents departed to Paradise. Missing his parents was so 
devastating to the young Abanoub, that he was called the lamented boy for he 
was sorrowful for so long. Some might ask wonder how could he manage to 
withstand all the sufferings that he encountered later on and yet could not resist 
the loss of his parents. 
It is true that despite our faith in heavenly life, it will not strip us from our 
human feelings; instead, it would sanctify them. We can see an illustration of 
that in the presence of St. Paul, who wrote about the door being opened for 
evangelism in Troas, and yet he could not find peace in his soul, for he could 
not find his friend Titus, so he left the city. "Furthermore, when I came to Troas 
to [preach] Christ's gospel, and a door was opened to me by the Lord, I had no 
rest in my spirit, because I did not find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave 
of them, I departed for Macedonia” (2 Cor. 2:12-13). This situation shows the 
vulnerability of human nature, and God may allow those weaknesses to prevent 
us from boasting. Another example of weakness was with our  great father 
Abraham, who said that his wife Sarah was his sister for fear that the king 
might kill him to take her for a wife (Gen. 20:2). Also, our beloved St. Mark, 
who left Paul and Barnabas and caused them to have an argument and ended 
up separating from each other (Acts 13:3), and St. Peter, who was leaving 
Rome for fear of persecution and Jesus appeared to him too and kindly 
corrected him. Therefore, we should not be troubled when we show weakness 
despite the grace given to us, for it is beneficial in keeping us humble and 
urging us to ask God to work in us and with us. 
In the village's church: 
One day, Abanoub went to the church and heard the priest during the sermon 
encouraging the congregation to endure with joy the suffering and persecution 
they were getting for their faith. After the Holy Communion, the young 
Abanoub went home, while the priest’s words still ringing in his ears.  
At home, he knelt to pray, asking for God ’s guidance. Then, he stood up 
and started walking towards the city of Semeno od (about 12 miles away), 
while rejoicing in the spirit and desiring to have the heavenly crown. 
In Semenood:

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 35
passages.text:
35 
 
At this point, the governor asked Abanoub to pray for him so that he and his 
soldiers could be healed. Abanoub told him that God would heal them in Atrib. 
When they got there, Abanoub prayed for the governor and treated him in the 
Lord’s name in the presence of Atrib ’s governor. This miracle caused many 
pagans to believe in the Lord, and some were martyred. 
In Atrib (Banha) 
Regardless, the governor of Atrib tortured Abanoub with all kinds of torture 
methods and put him in boiling oil and cut up his feet and hands and b linded 
his eyes with hot rods. During all these trials, God did not leave Abanoub, but 
He always sent Archangel Michael to heal him. Many witnesses became 
Christians and gladly became martyrs, from watching the young Abanoub 
enduring all that suffering and still praising his God. 
In Alexandria 
After the governor of Atrib saw the multitude of people accepting 
Abanoub's faith, he tied him up with reliable chains and sent him to Alexandria. 
There, he met a woman who had an evil spirit, and he forced the spirit  out of 
her, and she became Christian. Consequently, the soldiers killed her because 
she said that she believed in Christ.  
Abanoub continued to confess his faith in our Lord Jesus before the 
governor Arminius of Alexandria who also tortured him and put him in a room 
filled with snakes and serpents and the Archangel Michael got him out of it, 
and the snakes followed him, and one of them coiled itself around the 
governor's neck. He cried out to Abanoub, and he saved him, which caused 
many to believe and become martyrs.  
Abanoub suffered more tortures and was finally beheaded outside the city 
on a high rock where he stood to pray, asking God to forgive him and to accept 
his soul.  
St. Julius El-Akfahsy took his body and buried him in his town Nehissah, 
and wrote his story. His body was moved from Nehissah to Semenood, and the 
church celebrates his martyrdom on the 24th of Abib. 
 
ABANOUB, THE CONFESSOR, ST. 
The word ‘Abanoub’ is derived from the Coptic word ‘Pi-Noub’ meaning 
(gold). This saint was a virtuous mon k in one of the monasteries of Upper 
Egypt in the days of Diocletian, who tortured and shed the blood of 80 martyrs 
in a single day. 
It so happened when the name of St. Abanoub was mentioned before 
Arianius, the governor of Ansena, that the governor called him and asked him 
to worship the idols. The saint answered, saying: “How can I forsake my Lord

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 36
passages.text:
36 
 
Jesus Christ, and worship the idols made of stone?! ” Therefore, he tortured 
him severely, and then he sent him to the five western cities (the Pentapolis), 
where he was imprisoned for as long as seven years until Diocletian perished. 
When the righteous Emperor Constantine reigned, he gave his command to set 
free all those Christians who were in prisons and to bring them forth to him to 
have their blessing. He specified that in case it is difficult to bring them all, to 
bring only the prominent ones among them, such as ‘Zacharias Al-Ahnasy,’ 
Maximianus of Fayum, Agabius of ‘Dakhnin,’ and Abanoub of ‘Balaos.' The 
saints came out of their imprisonments, singing praises to God.  
At that time, St. Abanoub, the confessor, returned from ‘Pentapolis’ and 
dwelt on a mountain close to his homeland. When the Emperor’s envoy came, 
they took him on a boat to Ansena, where he encountered the believers, and 
the bishops ordained h im as a priest. And, it so happened that, while he was 
uttering: “The Holies are for the holy, ” that he saw the Lord Christ 
transfiguring in the church with His exalted glory.  
The Emperor’s envoy traveled together with 72 saints and put every two of 
them in a carriage, and while passing through one of the cities, where there 
was a nunnery of virgins, 700 of them came out singing hymns before them.  
When they reached the capital, the king sought from them to change their 
worn-out clothes to expensive new on es, but they declined his offer. He then 
kissed their wounds, honored them, and offered them precious gifts, which 
they also refused, except for some curtains and vessels for their churches, to 
which they returned, and St. Abanoub returned to his monastery. 
Finally, after fulfilling his strife, he reposed in peace. 
[Synaxarion, 23 Paona] 
 
ABASKHIRON AL-QUALINI 
(The martyr) 
The saint ’s name is derived from two words: The word ‘Abba’ means 
(Father) and the word ‘Skhiron,’ ‘Eskhirus,’ or ‘Eskaros,’ which means (the 
Strong). He was born in the town of ‘Qualin’ in the governorate of ‘Kafr El-
Sheikh’ in the Nile delta. He was a brave and beloved soldier, famous and 
appreciated by his leaders and fellow soldiers in the regiment that was camped 
in ‘Atrib’ (Benha). 
His position from the decree of Diocletian: 
Emperor Diocletian issued an order, mandating the sacrifice to idols by 
everybody all over his empire. When this decree was declared before the 
regiment’s soldiers, ‘Abaskhiron’ refused totally to obey. Then, the governor

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 34
passages.text:
34 
 
The young Abanoub went around the city and saw how the churches were 
destroyed, and the pagan cursed their neighbors the Christians for their fait h. 
He was distressed for what he saw and asked God to help him. God sent him 
Archangel Michael to assure him of the heavenly support and rewards that 
await him. He guided Abanoub to see the governor in the morning and declare 
his Christian faith and assure d him that he will be strengthened during his 
suffering and will be healed until he receives the crown of Martyrdom. 
What is the secret of his strength? 
1. While the names of his parents were not mentioned, the beauty of his 
parent’s faith was reflected on their only son Abanoub and provided him with 
hope in eternal life with our Lord. 
2. No doubt that his parents were sustaining him with their prayers before 
the throne of God. 
3. The pious priest who touched Abanoub's life and who encouraged his 
congregation not only to withstand the suffering and persecutions but also to 
accept it with a joyful heart, knowing that they will win the eternal kingdom. 
4. Heaven rejoiced for young Abanoub, and God has sent him Archangels 
Michael and Gabriel to support him. 
Before the governor: 
Early in the morning, Abanoub got up to see the governor and tell him 
openly about his faith. This action surprised the governor, who initially treated 
him nicely and promised him to be rewarded if he renounces his faith. 
Nevertheless, Abanoub was steadfast in his conviction of the true faith. The 
governor got furious that he could not sway a little boy like Abanoub, and he 
ordered him to be whipped so hard on his belly; that his intestines did come 
out. Archangel Michael appeared and heal ed him. Then, they throw him in 
prison, and all the Christian captives there were so happy to see him and were 
encouraged because of his strong faith and lack of fear.  
The next day the governor killed about 1000 of the prisoners, and they all 
received the crown of Martyrdom.  
On the following day, the governor called for Abanoub and ordered that he 
would be tied by his feet and hanged from the top of the mast of the boat that 
was sailing to Atrib [Banha] (about 40 miles away). He was mocking him, 
saying, "Let us see if his Jesus will come to save him." Moreover, they kept 
sailing from morning until evening. Finally, they brought the mast down, and 
the governor sat down to eat, and suddenly his hands were paralyzed, and his 
soldiers were hit with blindness. Suddenly, the governor did see the Archangel 
Michael coming closer to Abanoub, and he wiped the blood from his mouth 
and nose and released him from the ropes around his feet and brought him to 
the front of the boat, then the angel disappeared.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 52
passages.text:
52 
 
the entire night in the church, attending the Holy Liturgy in the early morning, 
partaking of the Holy Communion, and then he would go back to his cave. 
His Scribing: 
The saint was gifted with beautiful handwriting in both Coptic and Arabic 
languages. He preoccupied himself with copying so many ancient books. He 
also authored so many new books. Besides, he cared for binding the books and 
making leather gir dles and Eskeems. In addition to all those preoccupations 
and seclusion, he was the father of confession for all the monks of the 
‘Baramus’ monastery. 
Finally, Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih El-Masoudy’ reposed in peace on the 11th of Tout 
1621 AM (21 December 1905), at the age of 88 years. He was a monk for 71 
years in the monasteries of ‘Moharraq,’ ‘Baramus’ and in seclusion. 
[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 5, p. 106] 
 
ABD-JESUS THE BISHOP AND HIS COMPANIONS, SS. 
(The martyrs) 
In the days of the king of Persia ‘Shapur II’ (309-379 AD), around the year 
361 AD, five who carried the same name “Abd-jesus’ (Hebed-Jesus) were 
martyred: one of them was a bishop, three priests, a deacon and a monk. 
Bishop ‘Abdjesus,’ along with another bishop called ‘Abdas’ and a third 
bishop named ‘Dausas,’ were led captives to the area of ‘Zabde,’ where they 
were martyred. 
[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. II, p. 23] 
 
ABDON AND SENNEN, SS. 
(The martyrs) 
Two Persian Christians who were martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ 
(249-251 AD). Their biography could be found under the letter “S." 
 
ABE-FAM (Bifam/Phoebammon) EL-TAHAWY 
(The martyr) 
Pagan parents raised this saint in the city of ‘Taha’ in Upper Egypt. When 
he was 12 years old, his father gave many gifts to the prince to let his son join 
the army. Abe -Fam (Bifam/Phoebammon) eventually became a prominent 
officer, known for his love of justice and his defense of the oppressed and the

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 29
passages.text:
29 
 
Besides, his brother ‘Aba-Bishai’ was martyred on the first day of the 
‘Nasie’ (The little month).  
 [The Synaxarion: 29 Paona] 
 
ABAHOR, THE MONK, ST. 
This father from ‘Abraht’ in the area of the ‘Ashmonein,’ was an elect monk 
who surpassed many saints in his worship. Loving solitude and living alone in 
the wilderness, he was envied by the devil who appeared to him and said: “In 
the wilderness, you can overcome me because you are there alone, but I 
challenge you if you are brave, go to Alexandria." He instantly set forth to 
Alexandria, where he stayed sometimes serving the prisoners. 
It so happened that some horses were galloping in midtown, and one of 
them knocked down a little kid who instantly died. As St. Abahor was standing 
at the place where that incident took place, the devil provoked some people 
around to shout aloud, claiming that it was the old monk who killed him. When 
many started to revile and to scoff him, St. Abahor calmly took the kid to his 
bosom, prayed in his heart t o the Lord Christ, and then made the sign of the 
cross on him. The kid came back to life, and he gave him to his parents. Those 
around him glorified God and started to make it up to the old monk, who, 
fearing from the vainglory, he fled to the wilderness, where he dwelt for days 
in a monastery. 
When it was time for him to depart from this world, he saw a group of saints 
calling him to join them, for which he greatly rejoiced, became joyful, called 
his spiritual disciples to inform them that he will soon depart to the Lord Christ, 
and provided them with his last commandment. Hearing that, they much 
grieved that they will be orphans after his departure. He felt sick for a little 
while, and then he delivered his soul in the Lord’s hand. 
 [The Synaxarion: 2 Kiahk] 
 
ABAHOR 
(The martyr) 
He was born in ‘Seriakos’ to a father who was a blacksmith. Deciding to die 
a martyr, he set forth to ‘Al-Farma’ (nowadays: ‘Port Said ’), where he 
confessed the Lord Christ before its governor. The governor tortured him but 
much astonished at how the Lord came to comfort him and heal his wounds. 
Therefore, the governor, together with his entire household, proclaimed their 
faith in the Lord Christ. Accordingly, they were martyred by the hands of the

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 287
passages.text:
287 
 
BADABA, ABBA 
(The martyr) 
This saint was born in the city of ‘Armant’ in the governorate of ‘Qena,’ to 
a pious f amily; his father was called ‘Mina.’ The name ‘Badaba’ is derived 
from the Hieroglyphic word ‘Batby’: meaning (the principal/the essential) and 
from the Coptic word ‘Bataby’: meaning (related to the head). 
A strong friendship developed between this saint a nd his cousin ‘Andrew,’ 
who was two years older. Since their childhood, both carried the same love for 
the heavenly Kingdom; they encountered one another on the level of the spirit, 
despised the pleasures of the world, concentrated on the study of the Holy  
Scriptures and religious books, used to fast two consecutive days with no food 
or drink, in addition to praying day and night. 
Their Monastic Life: 
They set forth together to the Eastern mountain at ‘Qasr el-Sayyad’ in the 
district of 'Nagh Hamadi.' There, they became disciples of St. abba ‘Isaac’ and 
dwelt in a cell where they performed their spiritual practices. They took upon 
themselves to copy down the religious manuscripts for their spiritual benefit 
and to sell them for little money to cover their living expenses and to give what 
was left to the poor. 
As the sweet fragrance of Christ spread from them, their cell became a 
center of spiritual radiation. Abba ‘Tadros,’ the bishop of the area, came to 
them and ordained St. ‘Badaba’ as a priest and Andrew as a deacon. They used 
to perform the holy Liturgy once every forty days in a neighboring church. 
It so happened that abba ‘Tadros’ once entered into that church, and he saw 
the face of St. ‘Badaba’ shining with an amazing splendor and a crown as 
though of gold on his head. So, he longed to have him and deacon ‘Andrew’ to 
stay with him in the diocese. However, St. ‘Badaba’ excused himself and 
returned to his cell, whereas ‘Andrew’ consented to do so. And, when St. 
‘Badaba’ perceived that everyone was chasing him, he fled away from his cell, 
which the bishop dedicated as a church, later on. 
His Continuous Travels: 
Despite the escape of the saint, his virtues drew many people to continue 
chasing him, something that terrified him and forced him to double on his  
asceticism to chastise himself. He kept moving between ‘Ho,’ ‘Kos,’ ‘Naqada,’ 
and ‘Bahgura’ trying to get away from people. And, God, through him, kept 
doing amazing miracles. 
Bishop of ‘Qift’: 
After the repose of the bishop of ‘Qift,’ the clergy and the congregation,

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 296
passages.text:
296 
 
glorify him in a big way that people could not anymore look at his face because 
of all the exalted glory that shone out of it. People used to compare him to what 
happened to the prophet Moses. 
 
BANAMON, ST. 
The Church celebrates the feast of the repose of St. ‘Bioukha’ and St. 
‘Banamon’ (Banayen/Tayaban), on the 1st day of Abib. They were two saintly 
priests of the church of ‘Tuna’ in the province of ‘Tenda,’ whom God granted 
the grace of performing miracles and healing the sick. Their father was the 
overseer of the church, and he was a pious man.  
While St. ‘Banamon’ was serving the Divine Liturgy, he was told that his 
father, who was giving his last breath, wanted to see him. However, he said to 
them that, as long as he is dressed in the priestly service attire, it would not be 
befitting of him to leave the church. A fter calling on him three times, St. 
‘Banamon’ said, “If God wants me to see him before he departs, I will. But, let 
it be according to His will.”  
After the Holy Liturgy was concluded, he went to find his father already 
reposed. He was intensely grieved, and in particular, because his father was the 
only one who kept the vessels of the altar. Then, his brother advised him to go 
to the Fathers of the wilderness to seek their counsel. There, he met with St. 
‘Daniel’ who introduced him to another saintly brother who told him where to 
find the vessels.  
St. ‘Balamon’ lived with his brother St. ‘Bioukha’ in holy pious lives, until 
they completed their strife in the Lord. 
 
BANINA AND BANAO 
(The martyrs) 
‘Banina’ was raised in ‘Terot Saraban’ in Upper Egypt, withi n a pious 
family that feared God. While he was still young, his mother asked his father 
‘Abhata’ to send him to her brothers in the city of ‘Ansena’ to be trained under 
a skillful mentor. They all crossed the river, and there her brothers rejoiced 
greatly to have him. 
The boy showed a vast superiority that drew the attention of many, yet it 
stirred up the envy of one of his fellow pupils. That fellow took advantage of 
the absence of their teacher, and he broke the plate of the boy and threw it 
away. He also  bent the boy ’s fingers so violently that the boy lost 
consciousness. When the boy regained his senses, he outlined in great pain 
crying to his uncles; and he asked them to let him go back to his parents. At

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 56
passages.text:
56 
 
built outside the town of ‘Tema,’ whose all inhabitants were Christian. But, 
with the growing construction, it became inside the city towards its southern 
border, in the middle of its cemeteries. 
[Nabil Selim and Guirgis El-Meniawy: St. John the Herculean & the Three Saintly 
Abe-Fams, June 1966] 
 
ABE-FAM, ST. 
(The martyr) 
The young boy ‘Abe-Fam’ (Bifam/Phoebammon) was the uncle of prince 
‘John the Herculean, ’ who kept his company in particular at the time of his 
martyrdom in Upper Egypt.  
The young prince John refused to be a partner with Emperor Diocletian 
(284-305 AD) in his empire through wedding the sister of his wife. Prince John 
sharply and bravely rebuked Diocletian for his turning against the Christian 
faith. Besides, when the emperor sent him to Egypt to renovate the temples of 
the idols, he just destroyed those temples and left them in ruins. He also 
testified to his Christ before ‘Ariana,’ the governor of Ansena. Eventually, he 
was fiercely tortured and was finally martyred.  
His young uncle ‘Abe-Fam’ was just a 10 years old boy, and he mourned 
him bitterly saying: “Woe me, after your departure my beloved John; for when 
you were in the body I used to have comfort in your presence with me; and my 
heart held fast whenever  I looked at your face. ” A voice came out of John ’s 
dead body, saying: “My beloved Abe -Fam, if you like to become a martyr, 
leave my body here and hasten to catch the governor in the city of Assiut to 
write down your case. Behold, the Lord ordered to have your body put together 
with mine, whereas your soul will be with me; I shall receive it with the hosts 
of saints. ” On hearing this, the young boy hastened and caught ‘Ariana’ in 
Assiut and cried out, saying, “I am Christian” and made on himself the sign of 
the Cross. In anger, ‘Ariana’ ordered to torture him and cut his head off, on the 
5th of Paona. 
 
ABERCIUS, Fr. 
He lived in ‘Phrygia Salutris ’ in the second century, as a bishop on 
‘Heropolis’ (other than Hierapolis). He made a trip to Rome when he was 72 
years old, going through Syria and Mesopotamia, where he visited ‘Nusaybin.' 
God granted him grace in the eyes of everyone wherever he went. He baptized 
many people and performed the Sacrament of the Eucharist in many places. 
On his return home, he prepare d a tomb for himself, on which he engraved

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 30
passages.text:
30 
 
governor who followed him. The new governor, being tired of torturing St. 
Abahor, he sent him to Ansena, where he was tortured by the hinbazeen, was 
crucified upside down, burned by fire, etc. They finally cut his head off, and 
he received the crown of martyrdom. [The Synaxarion: 13 Abib] 
 
ABAKIR AND JOHN 
(The martyrs) 
Two Christian personalities: the first represents a man who is successful in 
his life, having been a skillful physician, beloved in his community and pious 
in his inner life, fulfilling the apostolic commandment: “Beloved, I pray that 
you may prosper in all things, and be in health, just as your soul prospers” (3 
John 1:2). The second one represents the active human being who lives 
stronger from within and seeks friendship to support him and to kindle his 
spirit. In other words, he was a serious man, asked even in his friendship, what 
was for the improvement of his soul. 
St. Abakir’s upbringing: 
He was born in Alexandria from pious parents, who cared for his spiritual 
life, and for his scientific and philosophical culture. There fore, he became a 
competent physician in his early youth, beloved and famous because of his 
faithfulness, piety, and virtue. 
The governor ‘Syrianos’ felt threatened by the saint as a Christian bearing 
a truthful testimony to his faith. He sought to kill hi m, charging him of being 
a magician, a sorcerer, and an evildoer. Hearing about this, Abakir escaped 
from Alexandria, according to the commandment of his Lord, saying, “When 
they persecute you in this city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23). 
His asceticism: 
He set forth to the Arabian mountains to dwell among the hermits 
meditating in the love of God, yet not disregarding his job as a physician. 
There, his fame spread to reach Palestine, Syria, and Mesopotamia. 
St. John: 
He was an officer in the army in the pr ovince of ‘El-Roha’ (Edessa) in 
Mesopotamia. Longing to a life of recluse and dedication for worship, and 
hearing about St. Abakir, he resigned from his work, and set forth to Jerusalem 
to visit the holy places; and from there he set forth to the desert to  meet with 
St. Abakir the hermit, with whom a close friendship grew on the level of the 
spirit; each of them supporting the other.

records.question: What is prayer, and why does God sometimes delay answering it?
records.answer:
Prayer is fundamentally described as "the converse and union of man with God," serving as a vital means of communication and connection with the Divine. It is not merely a ritualistic act but a profound engagement that upholds the world and fosters reconciliation with God. St. John Climacus elaborates on this by stating that prayer is "the food of the soul, the enlightenment of the mind, an axe against despair, a demonstration of hope, a cure for sorrow" [6]. This highlights the multifaceted nature of prayer, which encompasses not only requests but also a deep relational aspect with God.

In terms of why God sometimes delays answering prayers, several insights are provided by Church Fathers. St. Basil the Great explains that God may delay responses to prayers to increase the believer's zeal and desire to approach Him, allowing them to appreciate the gifts they receive more fully. This process helps individuals guard the blessings they obtain, as "that which a person receives with great effort, he strives to protect" [1]. Similarly, St. Augustine notes that delays can serve to teach the value of God's gifts, suggesting that "things which have been long desired are obtained with the greater pleasure" [1]. 

Moreover, it is essential to understand that God is aware of our needs even before we ask. Therefore, prayer is not about informing God but about aligning ourselves with His will and seeking what is truly good for us. St. Basil emphasizes that we should ask for things that are beneficial and for the kingdom of heaven, and that sometimes, what we request may not be appropriate for our spiritual growth [8]. 

In summary, prayer is a vital and dynamic interaction with God that nurtures our spiritual life, while delays in answers can serve to deepen our faith, teach us patience, and ensure that our requests align with God's greater wisdom and love for us.

“Abba Macarius was asked, ‘How should one pray? ’ The old man said, ‘There is no 
need at all to make long discourses; it is enough to stretch out one ’s hands and s ay, “Lord, 
as you will, and as you know, have mercy. ” And if the conflict grows fiercer say, “Lord, 
help!” He knows very well what we need and he shews us his mercy.’”46  
Abba Isaac says, “For so far will one be heard and obtain an answer, as he believes that 
he is regarded by  God, and that God can grant it. For this saying of our Lord cannot be 
retracted: ‘Whatsoever you ask when you  pray, believe that you shall receive, and they 
shall come to you’ (Mark 11:24).”47  
St. John Cassian says, “He is quite certain that his prayers will not be answered. Who 
is this wretch? It is he who prays and does not believe that he will receive an answer.” 
899. What should you do if God answers your prayers for your brother or sister? 
St. John Climacus says, “Do not be puffed up if you have prayed for another and been 
heard, for it is his faith that has been strong and effective.”48 
900. Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He 
sometimes not answer them at all? 
St. Basil the Great says, “It may be that He delays answering a prayer so that your zeal 
and your desire to approach Him may be multiplied, and that you may appreciate the gift of 
God and guard it carefully when you have received it. That which a person  receives with 
great effort, he strives to protect, lest in losing it his labor will have been in vain.”49  
St. Augustine says, “He, who was not willing to give [the unjust judge  in Luke 18:2], 
gave what was asked, because the other did not faint in asking. How much more then shall 
that Good One give who exhorts us to ask, who is displeased if we ask not? But when at 
times He gives somewhat slowly, it is that He is showing us the value of His good things; 
not that He refuses them. Things which have been long desired, are obtained with the 
greater pleasure, whereas those which are given quickly, are held cheap.”50  
“Some things, indeed, we wish because we are in  Christ, and other things we desire 
because still in this world … Abiding, therefore, ourselves in Him, when His words abide 
in us we sh all ask what we will, and it shall be done unto us. For if we ask, and the doing 
follows not, what we ask is not connected with our abiding in Him, nor with His words

our continual remembrance of Him.”54 
Tertullian says, “Prayer is alone that which vanquishes God  [cf. Gen. 32:22–30; Matt. 
11:12]. But Christ has willed that it be operative for no  evil: He had conferred on it all 
its virtue in the cause of good. And so it  knows nothing save how to recall the  souls of the 
departed from the very path of death, to transform the weak, to restore the sick, to purge the 
possessed, to open prison-bars, to loose the bonds of the innocent. Likewise it washes away 
faults, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, consoles the faint -spirited, cheers the 
high-spirited, escorts travelers, appeases waves, makes  robbers stand aghast, nourishes 
the poor, governs the rich, upraises the fallen, arrests the falling, confirms the standing. 
Prayer is the wall of  faith: her arms and  missiles against the foe who keeps watch over us 
on all sides. And, so never walk we unarmed. By day, be we mindful of Station; by night, 
of vigil. Under the arms of  prayer guard we the standard of our General; await we 
in prayer the angel’s trump … What more then, touching the office of  prayer? Even the 
Lord Himself prayed; to whom be honour and virtue unto the ages of the ages!”55 
St. Hesychius of Jerusalem  says, “‘Oh, that I my request  may be fulfilled  before the 
Lord.’ Should my prayers ascend on high, my enemies would perish, and the righteous 
person would stand firm (Wisd . of Sol.  5:1); the net would be broken, and the bird would 
be liberated  and fly freely (Ps. 124:7) ; the oppressors would bow their heads , and the 
oppressed would rejoice (Matt. 5:10–12).” 
Second: Prayer propagates the spirit of inner joy. St. Cyril the Great says, “For it is, I 
affirm, the duty of those who set apart their lives for His service, not to be sluggish in their 
prayers, nor again to consider it as a hard and laborious  duty: but rather to rejoice, because 
of the freedom of access granted them by God; for He would have us converse with Him as 
sons with a  father. Is not this then a privilege worthy of being valued by us most highly? 
For suppose that some one of those possessed of great earthly power were easy of access to 
us, and were to permit us to converse with him with full license, should we not consider it 
as a reason for extraordinary rejoicing? What possible doubt can there be of this? When 
therefore God permits us  each one to offer our addresses unto Him for whatever we wish, 
and has set before those who fear Him an honor so truly great and worthy of their gaining, 
let all slothfulness cease that would lead men to an injurious silence therein; and rather let 
us draw near with praises, and rejoicing that we have been commanded to converse with the 
Lord and God of all, having Christ as our Mediator, who with God the Father grants us the 
accomplishment of our supplications. For the blessed Paul somewhere writes, ‘Grace be 
unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ ’ (2 Cor. 1:2) . 
And He somewhere Himself said to the holy apostles, ‘Hitherto you have asked nothing in

“God in his justice rejects iniquity, and does not accept sin (Job 14:17), but since He 
ministers our salvation,  He longs for man, the work of His hands. In the midst of distress, 
Job cries out to God but it is as though God cannot hear him. However, when it is time for 
the resurrection, God will call him to rise and Job will answer; thus he encounters God who 
longs for the work of His hands, for Job will bear the reflection of the glory of God upon 
him.” 
“You shall call  me, and I will answer You (Job 14:15) … For now so long as we are 
subject to corruption, we do not in any wise ‘answer’ our Creator, seeing that whereas 
corruption is far from incorruption, there is no similarity suitable to our answering. But of 
that change it is written  When He shall appear, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him 
as He is (1 John 3:2). Then therefore we shall truly ‘answer Go d,’ Who ‘calls,’ when at the 
bidding of the Supreme Incorruption we shall arise incorruptible; and because the creature 
is not able to earn this by itself, but it is brought to pass by the gift of Almighty God alone, 
that it should be changed to that excee ding glory of incorruption, it is rightly subjoined: 
You will stretch forth Your right hand to the work of Your hands.  
“As if he said in plain words ; ‘For this reason Your corruptible creature is able to hold 
fast unto incorruption,  because he is lifted u p by the hands of Your power, and is kept by 
the grace of Your regard, that he should hold fast. ’ For the human creature by this alone, 
that it is a creature, has it inherent in itself to sink down below itself, but man has obtained 
it from his Creator, that he should both be caught above himself by contemplation, and held 
fast in himself by incorruption  [cf. 1 Cor. 15:53] . And so that the creature may not fall 
away beneath himself, but hold on in incorruption, he is lifted to the steadfastness of 
immutability by the right hand of His Maker  … who can estimate the bountifulness of 
Divine Mercy, that He should bring man after sin to such a height of glory? God takes 
account of the bad things we do, yet by the grace of His lovingkindness He remits them to

unable to be present before Him as you ought. If you commit yourself to this, you will not 
leave Him until you receive. If you do not receive what you ask, this is because your 
request was inappropriate or lacking in faith , or because you offered your prayer 
negligently, or because you ask for things that are not good for you, or because you ceased 
from praying . Oftentimes, people ask: Why do we pray? Is God ignorant of our needs ? 
Without doubt, He knows, and He gives us abundantly all temporal things even before we 
ask. However, we should first ask for the things that are good and for the kingdom of 
heaven, and thereafter we receive what we desire; but let us ask patiently and faithfully, ask 
for what is good for us, and let us not hinder our prayers by disobeying our consciences.”67 
St. Cyril the Great  says, “It is our duty  therefore to ‘pray without ceasing ’ (1 Thess. 
5:7), according to the words of the blessed Paul, as well knowing, and being thoroughly 
assured, that He Whom we supplicate is able to accomplish all things.  ‘For let a man’ it 
says, ‘ask in faith, in nothing divided: for he who is divided is like a wave of the sea, 
troubled and blown about by the wind. For let not,’ it says, ‘that man think tha t he will 
receive anything of the Lord’ (James 1:6–9) … for if you do not believe that He will incline 
unto you, and gladden you, and fulfill your request, do not draw near to Him at all … But 
that God will incline His ear to those who offer Him their prayers, not carelessly nor 
negligently, but with earne stness and constancy, the present parable assures us. For if the 
constant coining of the oppressed widow prevailed upon the unjust judge, who feared not 
God, neither had any shame at men, so that even against his will he granted her redress 
(Luke 18:1–8), how shall not He Who loves mercy, and hates iniquity, and Who  ever gives 
His helping hand to them that love Him, accept those who draw near to Him day and night, 
and avenge them as being His elect?”68 
Fifth: Leave matters in God’s hands. St. Augustine believes that the secret behind God 
answering David’s prayers and giving ear to the words of his mouth (Ps. 54:2) is that David 
surrendered matters into God’s hands; leaving decisions in His hands: “For sick you are; do 
not dictate to the physician the medicines he may choose to set beside you. If the teacher of 
the Gentiles, Paul the Apostle, says, ‘For we do not know what we should pray for as we 
ought’ (Rom. 8:26) how much more we? ”69 He again says, “Let not a sick man draw back 
from the hands of the physici an, let him not give advice to the physician. So it is with all 
these things temporal.”70 
Sixth: Ask faithfully, not quarrelsomely. St. Augustine says, “Now the wholesomeness 
of faith is this, that it makes us  seek, that we may find; ask, that we may receive; and

freedom of converse is born out of constant association with him.”43 
898. How can we offer prayer that is acceptable before God? 
The purpose of prayer is to keep the relationship between God and the person alive and 
effective. Therefore, we should consider the following when we pray: 
a. Trust in God who has complete love for humanity,  ability, wisdom, and knowledge 
(cf. Col. 2:2; Eccl. 8:17).  
b. Pray for the will of God in every matter, for He is the Pantocrator : “Thy will be 
done” (Matt. 6:10). 
c. Offer prayer from a heart that is unsoiled and pure.  
d. Begin every prayer with thanksgiving for the things that  God has granted us, for 
there is n o gift  that is not increased  except that which is received  without 
thanksgiving, according to St. Isaac the Syrian. 
e. Believe in the verse that says , “Unless the lord builds the house, they labor in vain 
who built it” (Ps. 127:1). 
f. Acknowledge that divine grace works in synergy with human striving. The Lord 
saved the child Moses and at the same time He rewarded the two midwives for 
ignoring pharaoh’s evil decree (Ex. 1:20).  
St. Basil the Great says, “There are conditions for a prayer to be answered : it must be 
according to the will of God (Matt. 26:39); we must be steadfast and persistent (Luke 11:8); 
we must realize that God’s wants us to reform our conduct , which is much more important 
than answering our prayers (Isa . 1:15); we must  be aware of  our unworthiness of that for 
which we ask (1 Chron. 17:4) or the unworthiness of those for whom we pray (Jer. 14:11); 
and that sometimes the lack of an answer to prayer is preferable to it being answered (2 
Cor. 12:7) … If all these conditions are met, then t here is no doubt that God will answer 
our prayers.”44 
Abba Zeno says, “If a man wants God to hear his prayer quickly, then before he prays 
for anything else, even his own soul, when he stands and stretches out his hands towards 
God, he must pray with all his heart for his enemies. Through this action God will hear 
everything that he asks.”45  
 
43 St. Isaac of Nineveh, On Ascetical Life (PP 11).

(Liturgical Press, 1984) Zeno 7: p. 65.

The Life of Prayer 
896. What is prayer? 
St. Clement of Alexandria says , “Prayer is, then, to speak more boldly, converse with 
God.”37  
St. John Climacus says, “Prayer by reason of its nature is the converse and union of 
man with God, and by reason of its action upholds the world and brin gs about 
reconciliation with God  … it is … a work of angels, the food of all the bodiless spirits , 
future gladness, unending activity, a source  of virtues, a means of obtaining  graces, 
invisible progress, food of the soul, the enlightenment of the mind, an axe against despair, a 
demonstration of hope, a cure for sorrow.”38  
“Let your prayer be completely simple. For both the publican and the prodigal son were 
reconciled to God by a single phrase.”39  
“The benefit of prayer can be inferred from the assaults of the demons during the divine 
service; and its fruit from the defeat of the foe.”40 
St. Basil the Great  says, “Thus will you pray without ceasing, if you not only pray in 
words, but unite yourself to God through all the course of life so that your life be made one 
ceaseless and uninterrupted prayer.”41  
The Letter to Diognetus says of Christians that “their days are passed on the earth, but 
their citizenship is above in the heavens.”42

Fourth: The silent prayer of a pure heart: “We may come to the prayer of silence which 
Hannah, the mother of Samuel, prayed (1 Sam. 1:13). It was acceptable before God, it 
opened up her barren womb and caused her shame to depart, and she gave birth to a 
Nazirite and a priest (1 Sam. 1:10–16).”261 
947. What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?  
St. Clement of Alexandria says, “Prayer is, then, to speak more boldly, converse with 
God. Though whispering, consequently, and not opening the lips, we speak in silence, yet 
we cry inwardly. For God hears continually all the inward converse.”262 
St. Aphrahat says , “Again our Savior taught the prayer and said, ‘You should pray 
secretly to the Hidden One; He sees everything’ (Matt. 6:6). For he said, ‘Enter the inner 
chamber and pray secretly to your Fathe r, and the Father who sees in secret will reward 
you’ (Matt. 6:6). But why, my beloved, did our Savior teach and say, ‘Pray to your Father 
in secret with the door closed?’ I will explain this to you as much as I have understood. For 
he said, ‘Pray to your Father in secret with the door closed.’ What is the door that he said to 
close? If not your mouth, which is (the door to) the temple in which Christ dwells as the 
Apostle said, ‘You are the temple of the Lord’ (1 Cor. 3:16), for him to enter into your 
inner man, to this house, cleanse it from everything that is unclean, while the door, that is 
your mouth, is to be closed. If that was not so, how would you understand this matter? For 
if it happens to you that you were in a land, and there is no house and doo r, would you not 
pray in secret? Or if it happens to you again that you were on the top of a mountain, would 
you not pray?  
“And our Savior showed this that God knows the will of the heart and of the thought, 
just as our Lord said, ‘Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him’ (Matt. 6:8). 
It is written in the prophet Isaiah, ‘Before they who were chosen by me call, I will hear 
them, and before they make the cry I will answer them’ (Isa. 65:24). Isaiah said again about 
the wicked, ‘Even though you mu ltiply prayer I will not listen’ (Isa. 1:15). He said again, 
‘They may cry in my ears with a loud voice, but I shall not hear them’ (Ezek. 8:18). But he 
said this about deceitful prayer, which is not accepted. For you must hear with excellence 
all the words, then you will understand their power.”263

904. Why do we pray? Does God not know what we need? 
St. Basil the Great  says, “He undoubtedly knows  [what we need]  and He gives us 
abundantly all temporal things even before we ask. However, we should first ask for the 
things that are profitable and for the kingdom of heaven, and thereafter we receive what we 
desire; but let us ask patiently and faithfully, ask for wh at is good for us, and let us not 
hinder our prayers by disobeying our consciences.”84 
905. Are communal prayers necessary?  
The believer feels that he is in communion with his brothers and sisters in prayer even 
in his private room, and thus he prays for all and asks for their prayers on his behalf. St. 
Basil wrote to one of the widows , “ be mindful of  God and have the fear of Him in your 
heart, and invite all to a union with you in your prayers. For great is the assistance of those 
who are able to move God.”85  
St. Ambrose says, “ For if according to the Lord ’s saying , that that which two shall 
have agreed upon on earth concerning anything which they shall ask, shall be done for 
them, as He says, by My Father, Who is in heaven, for: ‘Where two or three are gathered 
together in My Name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matt. 18:19) … how much less, 
where the full congregation is gathered in the Name of the Lord. Where the demand of all is 
unanimous, ought we to doubt that the Lord Jesus is there as the Author of that desire, and 
the Hearer of the petition.”86  
“Believe, then, that the Lord Jesus is present at the invocation of the  priest, Who 
said: ‘For where two or three are , there I am also’ (Matt. 18:20). How much where 
the Church is, and where His Mysteries are, does He vouchsafe to impart His presence!”87 
906. Is it helpful to prolong prayer? 
St. Augustine says, “In view of this, it is not reprehensible or useless to pray at length 
when one is free, that is, when the obligations of other good and necessary works do not 
prevent us, although even in those, as I said, we must always pray by that desire of the 
heart.”88 
907. What does the Lord Christ mean by saying, “ask … seek … knock” (Luke 11:9)? 
St. Augustine says, “In order that these three things —viz. asking, seeking, knocking—
may be made clear, let us suppose, for example , the case of one weak in his limbs, who

vine, because it draws not its life from the root.”51 
Abba Isaac, the disciple of St. Anthony,  says, “We sometimes ask for things opposed 
to our salvation and that we are most providentially refused our requests by Him who sees 
what is good for us with greater right and  truth than we can. And it is clear that this also 
happened to the teacher of the  Gentiles when he  prayed that the messenger of  Satan who 
had been for his good allowed by the Lord ’s will to buffet him, might be removed, 
saying: ‘For which I besought the Lord thrice that he might depart from me. And He said to 
me, My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness ’ (2 Cor. 12:8–
9).”52  
Pope Gregory the Great  says, “why is it that Paul three times besought the Lord and 
did not merit to be heard, but was told: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made 
perfect in weakness  (2 Cor. 12:9). Did the great preacher not ask in the name of the Son? 
Then why didn’t he r eceive what he asked? … The Son’s name is Jesus. Jesus means 
‘saviour’ or ‘saving.’ One who asks in the Saviour’s name asks what pertains to actual 
salvation. If what he asks for is not for his good he is not asking the Father in Jesus’ name. 
Hence the Lord says to his apostles while they were still weak, Up to now you have asked 
nothing in my name  (John 16:24) … That is the reason too why Paul was not heard. If he 
had been freed from temptation it would not have been of help to his salvation … consider 
your requests, I beseech you, and see if you are asking in the name of Jesus, if you are 
asking for the joys of eternal salvation … Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and 
all these things will be given you as well (Matt. 6:33).”53 
901.  What are the effects of prayer? 
First: The soul is inflamed with the love of God. St. Basil the Great says, “Prayers, too, 
following reading, take hold upon a fresher and more vigorous soul already stirred to a 
longing for God. And prayer which imprints in the soul a clear conception of God is an 
excellent thing. This abiding of God in our memory is the indwelling of God.  Thus we

Publications, 1990) 27: pp. 216–217.

St. Aphrahat says, “For God said through the prophet, ‘This is my rest, give rest to the

records.question: Why does the believer need to fast, and what is the purpose of fasting?
records.answer:
Fasting holds a significant place in the life of a believer within the Coptic Orthodox faith, serving multiple spiritual purposes. At its core, fasting is a means of spiritual growth and a way to draw closer to God. The believer needs to fast for several reasons, which can be synthesized from the teachings of the Church Fathers and the Catechism.

Firstly, fasting is seen as a way to express love and obedience to God. It recalls the original command given to Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, where they were instructed not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This command was not meant to deprive them but to encourage them to choose life and obedience, symbolized by the tree of life. St. Basil the Great emphasizes that “fasting began in Paradise” and that it serves as a way to declare our love for God, transcending earthly desires [1]. 

Moreover, fasting is described as a "medicine of the soul," helping to rid it of sin and prepare it for a deeper relationship with God. St. Basil notes that fasting is a guardian of the soul and a companion for the body, equipping believers to resist temptations and grow in piety [1][2]. It is also a way to prepare for spiritual warfare, as it strengthens the believer against sin and distractions [7].

The purpose of fasting extends beyond mere abstention from food. It is a practice that cultivates virtues, motivates gratitude, and fosters an appreciation for the blessings of food. St. Jerome states that fasting is “not itself an absolute virtue, but the foundation of virtues” [4]. By fasting, believers become more aware of God’s grace and learn to appreciate the simple blessings in life. St. Basil further explains that fasting enhances the enjoyment of food when it is partaken after a period of abstinence, allowing believers to rejoice in God’s provisions [4].

Fasting also serves as a preparation for the believer's ultimate union with Christ, referred to as the "Bridegroom." As Christ stated, “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. 9:15). Fasting is a way to adorn oneself spiritually for the time when the Bridegroom returns, emphasizing the longing for communion with God [2]. 

In summary, fasting is essential for believers as it fosters obedience, cultivates virtues, prepares the soul for spiritual warfare, and enhances the appreciation of God’s blessings. It is a multifaceted practice that ultimately aims to deepen one's relationship with God and prepare for eternal life with Him.

Holy Fasting 
1015.  Why does the believer need to fast? 
God — who created everything for the humans  that He might make of them living 
kings queens — gave the humans  one commandment : not to eat of the tree of the 
knowledge of good and evil. He did not do so to deprive them of anything but wanted them 
to stretch out their hands and eat from the tree of life, and so to live, through obedience, in a 
blissful eternity, like the holy angels. Moreover, A dam and Eve could have resisted Satan 
and all his soldiers through obedience to the divine commandment, and there by declare 
through their fast ing that their love for God transcends everything. The Lord planted for 
them the Garden of Eden (Gen. 2:8) to make of their hearts an exalted paradise. 
St. Basil the Great  says, “Fasting began in Paradise when God said to Adam: ‘Do not 
eat from the tree of knowledge of the good and evil. ’ Our first parents were driven out of 
Paradise for lack of fasting . Therefore, fa sting is the way to enter the kingdom. Do not 
tremble or be afraid of fasting . Does your body not need medicine? Likewise, your soul 
also often needs medicine. Fasting is the medicine of the soul, to rid it of sin.”412 
Also, in the Old Testament  deuterocanonical Book of  Judith, the leaders and people  
trusted that the Lord would heed their prayers when they  were steadfast in fasting and 
prayers in the sight of the Lord (Judith 4:8–15). 
1016. What do the Church Fathers say about fasting? 
St. Basil the Great  says, “[Fasting] is a good guardian of the soul, a safe companion 
for the body, the best weapon, a training regimen for contestants. It drives away 
temptations. It readies for piety. It is the companion of sobriety and the craftsman of self -
control. In war it teaches bravery, in peace stillness. It sanctifies the Nazirite [monk] and 
perfects the priest. For it is impossible to venture upon priestly activities without fasting, 
not only in the case of our present holy and true worship, but als o in the prefigured worship 
set out in the law.”413 
“Fasting is likeness to the angels, companionship with the righteous, moderation in life. 
It made Moses the lawgiver. Samuel is the fruit of fasting. Hannah as she fasted vowed to 
God: O Lord God of Sabaot h, if you were to look upon your maidservant and give me a 
male child, then I will offer him in your presence as a gift. He shall drink no wine or strong 
drink until the day of his death  (1 Sam. 1:11 LXX). The great Samson was reared on 
 
412 See Elias Koyter al-Mukhlessy, St. Basil the Great (Arabic) (Publications of the Pauline Library in Beirut, 
1989): p. 288. 
413 St. Basil of Caesarea, On Fasting and Feasts 1.6 (PP 50:61).
